item.content:encoded:
Why: On your always-include list. (score 10)

From Cliff Mass Weather Blog.

There is a deep connection between meteorology and religion, and there are times when one wonders about divine intervention in our weather.

This is such a time.


Last year brought low snowpack for most of the West.  

Some were worried about water shortages and poor crops.   

But well-timed rain and substantial reservoir storage saved the day, with agriculture doing well and sufficient water available for human consumption.

Divine intervention?

This fall started out relatively dry, and some folks were worried, including a certain local newspaper.


But again, higher powers intervened.   During the past 72 hours, there have been substantial amounts of precipitation over the region (see below)


 A potent atmospheric river was the cause of our wet bounty (see below).  


Local reservoirs are refilling, including some low ones on the Olympic Peninsula (such as Wynoochee Lake below)


Other regions have been in need, and divine intervention has been and will be evident.

For example, California, the source of many of our fruits and vegetables.

Well-timed rainfall last year filled the reservoirs, but snowpack was low.   As a result, some of the big reservoirs are now below normal, such as Shasta and Oroville (see below).


Fortunately,  the current forecasts promise significant intervention, with massive amounts of precipitation over the Golden State during the next ten days (see below).   Remarkable.



This wet bounty includes LOTS of snow in the Rockies and over the drainage of the Colorado River (see below). A miracle.


Not getting religion yet?   What about British Columbia, which has suffered from a lack of precipitation this fall?    

Vancouver's reservoirs are quite low.


Fortunately, impressive amounts of precipitation are forecast for southwestern BC through next Monday morning



The water situation is rapidly improving on the West Coast.  The forecasts are highly promising.

There is only one thing to say about it:

item.content:encoded:
Why: A real-world CA key compromise leading to revoked intermediates is a key management lesson. (score 9)

From The Hacker News.

The in-house Python script behind eMudhra's October key compromise has now cost the company 8 more of its intermediate certificate authorities (CAs), even though it did not weaken their keys.

Each intermediate CA has its own private key, which the company uses to sign the certificates it issues. The 8 intermediate CAs compromised in October had a different problem: a single line in the script cut each of their keys to one byte, the company said this week.

The script also retrieved the RSA keys of the 8 newly revoked CAs from the company's hardware security modules (HSMs). The company says it cannot show that the keys were handled as required by its own rules. It revoked the CAs late last week.

The company had called those CAs unaffected. "The RSA issuers went through a different path as per our assessment of the code and are therefore not impacted," it wrote on Mozilla's bug tracker on October 19.

Of the 8, 6 were for website (TLS) certificates and 2 for code signing. The company had put 4 of them into production in May. Its list names 195 certificates from them, 29 for its own domains.

Both problems began at a key ceremony on April 30, 2025, according to the full incident report the company posted to the same bug tracker this week. That day it generated 16 CA keys on Utimaco HSMs, including the 8 behind the October key compromise.

The keys were meant for Crypto4A HSMs at the company's US and EU sites. Moving keys between HSMs from different vendors is limited, the company says, so its PKI operations team wrote the Python script to wrap each key for transport and unwrap it again.

The round trip that day was a practice run of the transfer, and the source HSM's FIPS-approved mode was switched off for it as an approved exception.

After the round trip, the script read each private key out of the HSM into the ceremony computer's memory and rebuilt the key from that copy. For the 8 ECDSA keys, "a single line in that read‑back truncated the private value to its leading byte," the report says.

The rebuilt key carried a label almost identical to the original's, which allowed the weak copy to be sent for signing and certification.

The Hacker News worked out all 8 keys from their public certificates. The smallest, for EM OV TLS CA - G3C, is 4, and the largest is 237.

Nothing in the ceremony tested the key's strength or checked the certified key against the first generated key. The weak keys still produced valid signatures, and their certificates passed linting and 2 WebTrust audit cycles unnoticed.

The HSMs worked correctly throughout, according to the company, which puts the fault in its own script and process controls.

Invalid CRL signatures in June 2025 were an early sign of the same fault, according to the report. The company fixed them at the time by re-signing the lists with the keys that matched the certificates, which were the weak ones.

According to the report, the 8 RSA keys went through the same read-back step that the company's earlier response had ruled out. Early last week, the company said its earlier answers reflected only what its teams had gathered so far, including which script paths each set of keys took.

The script did not shorten those keys, and every signature still checks against the certified key. But their private parts, such as the private exponent and one of the primes, sat in the memory of a Python process on the ceremony computer.

As a result, the company "cannot positively demonstrate that this key material was in compliance with CPS §6.2.6," its own rule on moving keys into and out of an HSM. Logs and files from that computer cannot reliably show how the material was handled.

The company reached that view in early November, after discussions with browser root programs. The 8 RSA CAs were revoked late last week with the reason code cessationOfOperation, not the CA-compromise code used when the first 8 were revoked on October 18.

Participants in the bug thread have asked why the company chose that code rather than keyCompromise.

Of the 195 certificates in the company's certificate list, 130 came from EM DV TLS CA - G2C, 63 from EM OV TLS CA - G2C, and 2 from the code-signing CA, EM OV CS CA - G2C.

Besides the company's own domains, the certificates name several universities and colleges, a county, and other organizations. The newest was issued last week, days before the CAs were revoked. All their holders have been moved to new certificates, the company says.

The company says the wrap-and-unwrap process was used only this once, and that its other key ceremonies all created keys in place.

Participants in the bug thread also want the script published, and some have asked how private keys could leave its HSMs at all.

KPMG, which the company hired as an independent reviewer, is due to finish by December 4. The company's inventory of all its CA keys is due November 30.

The company knows of no case of misuse. Anyone holding one of the October keys could have impersonated any website, according to a disclosure site run by Dennis Jackson, who investigated the keys for Mozilla.

Browsers that enforce Certificate Transparency could not have been fooled. Whether anyone used the keys against software that skips that check is not known.

What emSign Certificate Holders Need to Check

eMudhra, which sells certificates under the emSign brand, is exiting the publicly trusted TLS business following its October 22 announcement.

Holders can find affected certificates in the company's list or by searching Certificate Transparency logs for the revoked G2C TLS issuers.

All issuance from the company's G1 hierarchy is due to stop before November 16, as the remaining customers, mainly a university federation in North America, move to another provider.

Microsoft will start removing the 10 remaining eMudhra roots, including emSign Root CA - G1, on November 16, according to an update to its security response post earlier this week. Certificates that chain to those roots will then lose default trust in Windows and Edge, and in some of its other products on their own timelines.

According to the Indian company's phase-out schedule, Chrome and Firefox will not trust G1 certificates issued after November 16, and Apple will end trust in all G1 certificates, including older ones, on November 30.

macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3 stop bundled command-line tools such as curl and git from accepting the compromised TLS CA certificates, Apple said in a support note earlier this week. They also drop 5 roots, including emSign Root CA - G1, from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, so tools relying on that file may not verify some sites chaining to them.

Google News,

item.title: iFixit reveals the magic behind the new glowing MacBook Pro logo ↦
item.author: Six Colors
item.description:
Why: Six Colors on the engineering behind the glowing MacBook Pro logo, a thoughtful Apple hardware story. (score 8)

From Six Colors.

(Image: iFixIt) When I was in Los Angeles getting briefed on the MacBook Pro with PROLED, I asked Apple representatives directly about how they made the Apple logo on the back glow again, given that OLED displays don’t leak light out the back.…
item.content:encoded:
Why: Six Colors on the engineering behind the glowing MacBook Pro logo, a thoughtful Apple hardware story. (score 8)

From Six Colors.

When I was in Los Angeles getting briefed on the MacBook Pro with PROLED, I asked Apple representatives directly about how they made the Apple logo on the back glow again, given that OLED displays don’t leak light out the back.

They jokingly told me it was “magic,” said that it was actually hard work to do, and refused to get into details.

Okay, I said—I’ll just wait for iFixit to tear one apart.

On old MacBooks, light from the LCD backlight shone through an apple-shaped window in the lid. But the PROLED’s pixels make their own light. So, yes, Apple waited until the first MacBook Pro without a backlight to bring back the backlit logo.

Of course we had to get inside.

The result is pretty much what you’d expect:

Under a taped patch in the middle we found four LEDs, all in a strip along one edge. The light hits a reflective layer and passes through a diffuser, turning four little points of light into one evenly glowing apple. The logo itself has a mirror-like coating that looks shiny with the lights off.

(There’s also a YouTube video of the teardown.)

My favorite aspect of this new easter egg of a feature is that with the light off, you can’t tell that it’s the new MacBook Pro. It doesn’t look like the white logo cut-out of years past; it looks exactly like the mirrored metallic logos of the last decade. Except… then it lights up. Magic indeed.

Go to the linked site.

Read on Six Colors.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Microsoft research showing AI backdoors via editing under 10 neurons is relevant to security and AI. (score 8)

From The Hacker News.

An AI model can be given a hidden backdoor by editing fewer than 10 of its rarely used neurons, without retraining the model, Microsoft researchers have shown.

When a chosen trigger appears, the model outputs an attacker's command, which an agent using that model would run with the agent's own permissions. The attacker must be able to change the model's weights.

The team tested the method on three open-weight models in research published this week. Microsoft says it has not seen any threat actors use the technique. The company also published guidance on defending against it.

The edited neurons are ones that rarely fire and barely affect the model's answers. They were set to fire only when a trigger string appears, either in a user's request or later in a tool's output.

The researchers call the method Lazarus. Each edited neuron forces one token of the command into the model's output, so a command needs about one neuron per token.

The new neuron settings are calculated directly and can then be tuned with a few hundred training steps on those neurons alone. Nothing else in the model file or the code that runs it changes.

In a researcher's walkthrough posted on X, a backdoored Nemotron-Terminal-8B model with 10 edited neurons was tasked with fixing a Node.js server. It worked normally for three turns.

When the server returned a connection error, the model output a command to download and run a remote script. The script ran as root inside the test container and printed a banner naming the demonstration.

Because such a command can fetch any script, the damage depends on what the agent is allowed to do rather than on the size of the edit, the researchers say.

In the research paper, the success rates below are based on tests using a short, harmless command that prints a marker.

On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the team edited and tuned seven of the more than 12,000 neurons in the model's last feed-forward layer, using just 23 example sessions. The edited model output the command in at least 98.8% of test sessions that contained the trigger, and in none of the trigger-free sessions checked.

With the tuned version of the edit, success rates on Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT ranged from 51% to 99.5%, depending on the setup. The Qwen model used six neurons.

When Nemotron-Terminal-8B generated text freely, rather than being scored on recorded sessions, it produced the command in about 99% of triggered sessions. In one setup, the command also appeared in 0.14% of sessions without the trigger.

The edited models still pass ordinary tests, the researchers say. Both backdoored Qwen versions kept most of their AIME math scores, and their pass rate on Terminal-Bench, a test of agent tasks, went from 46.59% to 42.05%.

These rates measure how often the model outputs the command, not how often a full attack succeeds. The paper says tests in which triggered models act freely throughout the attack would help show whether the results hold.

Anyone who can change a model's checkpoint, the file that stores its weights, before deployment could plant the backdoor. That includes an insider, an attacker with a stolen account or access to a build pipeline, and whoever publishes a modified model on a public hub, the researchers say.

Planting it does not need the computing power of full training. The researchers also credit Claude Code, running the Opus 4.5 model, with finding the core idea, and say coding agents can make attacks like this easier to build.

Weight-level backdoors in agent models have been shown before. In an earlier proof of concept published on October 6, ProjectDiscovery researchers fine-tuned an open Qwen model to react to a trigger phrase. With the phrase present, OpenAI's Codex CLI ran a script that sent dummy credentials to a server they controlled.

Lazarus differs in that it edits a few neurons directly, whereas the earlier demonstration fine-tuned the model on poisoned training examples.

Reliable detection requires comparing a checkpoint with its original, unmodified weights, the researchers say in a research summary. Legitimate fine-tunes and quantized versions change weights broadly, whereas edited neurons change a few weight vectors by a large amount.

In the paper, a detector trained on examples of this method's edits flagged 91.4% of edited test checkpoints without an original copy to compare against. It also wrongly flagged 9.7% of clean ones. The test set was small, 35 edited and 31 clean checkpoints, and the detector was not tested on other kinds of backdoor edits.

Asking AI models to inspect a checkpoint directly worked less well. Claude Opus 5.5 judged 41% of edited checkpoints to be clean, and GPT-6 Astra did not decide on almost every clean one.

No scan can prove beyond doubt that a model is safe, the researchers say.

What Teams Running Agents Can Do

Microsoft's mitigation guidance includes these steps:

  • Compare every checkpoint with its declared base model before deployment and after each update, and reject models whose base cannot be checked.
  • Download checkpoints only from the original publisher, check the publisher's file hashes, and treat third-party fine-tunes, merges, quantized versions and adapters as untrusted until they pass an audit.
  • Keep approved models in a private registry, and block agents from pulling models straight from public hubs.
  • Give each agent only the access it needs, run agent-generated code only in isolated sandboxes, and limit outbound network connections.
  • Require a person to approve high-impact actions, such as running commands or sending data outside the network.
  • Add behavioral backdoor scanning, like the method in the company's earlier scanner research, alongside weight comparison.

Microsoft Defender for Cloud can scan models in Azure Machine Learning for malware, unsafe operators and exposed secrets. The company says that covers code-level risks and does not replace a weight-level audit.

Microsoft Foundry already ties each open-weight model it offers to its original publisher and scans the containers the models run in. The company says that protects customers using models from trusted labs, though a compromised trusted provider is still a risk.

The company is also building a red-teaming tool based on detection methods and exploring weight scanning for open-weight models that it adds to Foundry. It plans to sign models so customers can check where they came from.

Google News,

item.title: Nintendo Goes Back to the Zelda Well
item.author: Spyglass
item.description:
Why: Spyglass take on Nintendo reworking Ocarina of Time for Switch 2. (score 7)

From Spyglass.

'Ocarina of Time' should be the first of many reworks for the Switch 2...
item.content:encoded:
Why: Spyglass take on Nintendo reworking Ocarina of Time for Switch 2. (score 7)

From Spyglass.

Over the past few quarters, seemingly all videogame console makers have been in a rut. Some of it was out of their control – the memory chip and other component shortages have forced price-rises in a time when they might otherwise be dropping prices. Some of it was shooting themselves in the foot with stupid strategy for years – see: Xbox. But a lot of it just seems cyclical, hit games come and go but generally can't be timed, but it's exacerbated by the fact that the industry has been caught waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI, which has seen delay after delay after delay.

But Nintendo should have been largely immune to the first two, as the Switch was clearly the right strategy – including releasing a Switch 2 which follows the same model, but is just better – and tied to that is their fantastic IP which makes them more immune from needing a GTA-sized hit to move their consoles. And yet, Nintendo has been struggling too. Some of it is the pricing situation, but more of it is simply the slow-roll of new hit games. But again, Nintendo has that IP. And while it make take years to make a new Zelda game, you know what they can do faster (and cheaper)? Remake an old one:

Nintendo Co. sold 5.2 million copies of its The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake in just four days, invigorating the Switch 2 platform that had been waiting for a blockbuster hit.

Released on Nov. 5 for $59.99, the 2026 edition is a complete recreation of the 1998 classic action-adventure game for the Nintendo 64 console, replete with new graphics, level and character designs. It ranks among the best-reviewed video games of recent times, earning a score of 96 out of 100 from both players and professional reviewers on aggregator Metacritic.

It's a massive number of copies in a few days, but it shouldn't be a surprise. Ocarina of Time is widely considered to be one of the best games of all-time. That doesn't cease to be the case simply because it's old. At the same time, to entice the new generation of gamers, many of which were not alive 28 years ago when it was first released, you obviously need to update the game to be more "modern".

The only thing that surprises me is that it took Nintendo so long to stumble upon this strategy. I mean, I wrote about how they should do this almost 13 years ago – when they were last in a rut before the Switch came into being.1 As I wrote back then:

Step two of my strategy would involve updating old classics to run with updated HD graphics and new levels. New Mario. New Zelda. New Icarus. New Donkey Kong. New Pokemon. Same idea. Updated graphics. New levels. These games would be $15 to $25 depending on the game. Stagger them.

My only mistake was undercutting the price they could charge – by more than half! That was a silly mistake. It's not like Hollywood charges half the ticket price when they remake old hit movies.

Of course, remaking old games isn't entirely new, but Nintendo has historically focused on more minor updates to classic games, or made such revamps a smaller part of a bigger package with things like New Super Mario Bros. Part of the issue was that games from the 1980s were quite small in scope due to technology limits at the times. But as we got well into the 1990s, that scope expanded fast, and so games like Ocarina can warrant an actual full remake without it seeming a bit silly – as remaking a silent movie for a modern audience might be.

So perhaps we should consider this "new retro" gaming. Old, beloved games that don't rely solely on nostalgia, but can still hold up on their own with some fresh paint and updated controls for a more modern audience.2

It's sort of funny to think of Ocarina of Time as "retro" but it's 28 years old! A 28-year-old game that came out in 1998 when Ocarina was released would have been from 1970. There's no reason "retro" needs to only include 8-bit titles, of course. And so now Nintendo finally has a playbook – and a killer data point – for a lot more of this.3

1 To be clear, my main idea was to do a $99 retro console of sorts focused on these nostalgic games. Nintendo eventually sort of did this as well, though more down-the-middle mini versions of actual old consoles (which were cheaper and oddly meant as more of a novelty). ↩

2 Also useful when you have a big Legend of Zelda movie launching into theaters next year! ↩

3 To be clear, that can't just rely on these older titles being remade, obviously. But it's an easy and relatively cheap way to keep up momentum between big, fully new releases. Though that's a lesson Hollywood needs to relearn every so often. ↩

From Six Colors.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Apple shutting down its Support Community is notable Apple news, covered by a favorite writer. (score 7)

From Six Colors.

In a long-overdue move, Apple has brought down the hammer on its “Apple Support Community” forum. As Joe Rossignol at MacRumors reports:

Apple’s full notice added to the site: “The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site. We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.”

It is the end of an era. Apple offered an online discussion forum for user-to-user technical support since 1998, when it launched the Apple Tech Exchange. The forums were renamed to Apple Discussions in 2000, and then to the Apple Support Communities in 2011, before taking on their current Apple Support Community name in 2022.

Apple informed MacRumors that it decided to sunset the Apple Support Community after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs.

These message boards were an embarrassment for Apple. Not only were they very much out of step with what the web has come to be over the last couple of decades, but their presence under an apple.com domain meant that they ranked highly in search and were perceived by the general public as being official in some way.

But they weren’t, nor were they helpful. They were full of people asking questions and not getting useful answers, with many responses given by users who were more motivated to gain karma in the forum’s user-ranking system than to help. I can’t tell you how many times I visited these forums while trying to track down the answer to a peculiar quirk or bug, only to find the (legitimate!) question being shut down by an officious high-ranking know-it-all who didn’t actually understand what was being asked and couldn’t provide a useful answer.

Good riddance.

Go to the linked site.

Read on Six Colors.

item.title: AI proved a major quantum complexity conjecture. What does it mean?
item.author: Big Think

item.content:encoded:
Why: AI proving a quantum complexity conjecture ties to crypto and AI themes. (score 7)

From Big Think.

If you work with a normal computer — a classical computer — you’re used to two foundational ideas:

  • the idea of bits, where information gets encoded as a “0” or “1” within some sort of storage medium or mechanism,
  • and the idea of operations that can be performed on those bits (or “gates” that those bits can be passed through), which represent the possible computations that can be conducted with those bits.

Some problems can be solved very efficiently with classical bits and classical gates, like four-function (+, -, ×, ÷) mathematics, while other problems can only be solved extremely inefficiently with classical bits and classical gates, with the traveling salesman problem being a legendary example of such a “hard” problem.

If you bring in the additional possibilities associated with a quantum computer, however, you no longer have just classical bits and classical gates, but qubits and fundamentally quantum gates. One of the biggest questions in all of computer science is this: which questions and problems, and under which conditions, will the additional options provided by these qubits and quantum gates result in a major computational speedup, and by how much?

That speedup is known as either quantum supremacy or quantum advantage. Which useful problems will experience a quantum advantage, and by how much? That’s one of the main goals of the field of quantum complexity. One of the central open problems in that field, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, has just been solved: by an AI company. Here’s what it does — and doesn’t — mean.

What you see, above, is a map of what’s known as different complexity classes in computer science. Any computational problem is one where you can identify a problem, write down an algorithm for solving that problem, computationally execute that step-by-step algorithm for the specific input associated with that problem, and get an answer. That answer can be a simple binary (yes/no; true/false) answer, which comes for problems that are decision-type problems. However, computational problems include ones that require a more complex quantitative answer: a function problem, a counting problem, or an optimization problem (such as the traveling salesman problem) are all examples of problems more complex than decision problems.

One of the most important complexity classes is known as P. P contains all of the problems that can be solved in polynomial time: generally regarded as “efficiently solvable” problems. If you have a deterministic Turing machine, you can solve a problem of class P using a polynomial amount of computational time. If you’ve ever heard of the famed
P versus NP conjecture, it’s a debate over whether problems that are “NP hard,” or which seem to require a nondeterministic amount of polynomial time to solve, could actually ever be solved in polynomial time. It is one of the unclaimed Millennium Prize Problems.

Here’s an example that might help you understand the difference between P and NP: I’m going to give you a number, and we’re going to ask if this number is prime. As a simple example (yes, your computer can do this easily), we’re going to pick a relatively small number: 70,747. Is it prime? If we wanted to write an algorithm to determine whether it was prime, you can imagine:

  • dividing by 2,
  • dividing by 3,
  • dividing by 5,
  • dividing by 7,
  • dividing by 11,
  • dividing by 13,
  • dividing by 17,

and so on and so on, until you found a prime number that it was divisible by. Either you’d eventually find one, and so you’d know it wasn’t prime, or you would get to a number that was bigger than the square root of the number without finding one, and that would tell you it was prime.

For the number I gave you, 70,747, this algorithm would eventually find that it’s divisible by 263, and that when you divide 70,747 by 263, you find that its other divisor is 269. Finding out if 70,747 is a prime number is an example of an NP problem, but if I give you either 263 or 269, verifying that it’s not prime is easy: an example of a P problem. For much larger numbers — like 80-digit numbers, for example — the verification is easy if you know the counterexample, but demonstrating that an “actually prime” 80-digit number is prime is incredibly computationally difficult. It’s not something that, with today’s computational technology, we can easily or readily do.

Now that we know what different computational complexity classes are, we can turn to the other aspect to this problem: the difference between classical and quantum computers, and the hope of a “quantum speedup” for certain classes of problems. While classical computers are limited to bits and standard classical operations — operations such as AND, NOT, and OR — quantum computers have inherently quantum versions of both of these in addition to just the classical versions of what’s available.

The first major difference is that instead of just bits, which are always in a state that’s a “0” or a “1” with zero exceptions, qubits can also exist in an intermediate state. That intermediate state can be a superposition of “part 0” and “part 1” that isn’t necessarily either 100%/0%, 50%/50%, or 0%/100%, but any value in between them. As long as it sums up to 100% probability at every moment in time, all states are allowed. The amount of “0” and the amount of “1” that it has changes for three reasons:

  • as a result of operations performed on it,
  • as a result of a measurement of the state (which always collapses it to either a “0” or a “1”),
  • or as a result of time-evolution.

Of course, since this quantum computer isn’t a perfectly isolated environment, there are also sources of noise and errors from the surrounding particles in the system. Therefore, there are also errors introduced, so that the fidelity of your quantum computer is never perfect. Regardless, the fundamental principle holds: qubits can be a mix of “0” and “1” states combined.

There are also inherently quantum gates: gates that don’t just transform bits from their current state to the opposite state or allow them to remain the same, but rather can transform the qubit from any initial state to any final state in a way that conserves total probability. This can take on many forms.

  • There are Pauli gates, which are single-qubit gates that can perform bit-flips, phase-flips, or combinations of the two.
  • There are Hadamard gates, which are single-qubit gates that transform an initially pure state (a “0” or a “1”) into a mixed state that’s an equal superposition of both options.
  • There are CNOT gates, which are multi-qubit gates that use both a control qubit and a target qubit, flipping the target qubit depending on the state of the control qubit.

And there are many other gates as well that are inherently only available to quantum computers.

However, it’s important to recognize that you can always use a number of classical gates and operations in order to reproduce, simulate, or “hold enough information” to approximate any qubits and quantum gates to whatever level of precision you desire. While you might think that an inherently quantum system would require a quantum computer, with qubits and quantum gates, to model it, it’s been known for many decades that is not the case: the Church-Turing thesis dictates that any computable function can indeed be in-principle computed by a classical computer. There is no problem that absolutely requires a quantum computer in order to solve it.

But the Church-Turing thesis says nothing about the efficiency of that computability. There are some problems that might be extremely inefficient to solve on a classical computer but extremely efficient to solve on a quantum computer; it’s expected that physical quantum mechanical problems, like simulating the double-slit experiment, fall into this category. However, for a wide variety of problems, it’s unclear how much of a speedup a quantum computer can get you versus a classical computer.

Furthermore, because it’s so easy to have extraordinarily large numbers of bits — megabits, gigabits, terabits, petabits, etc. — on a classical computer, but difficult to maintain even a few dozen qubits for more than a tiny fraction of a second of coherence, even in cases where it’s possible to gain a quantum advantage, it’s incredibly difficult to gain a practical quantum advantage.

How complex is a computational problem, anyway? And what’s the difference between the complexity of a classically-stated problem versus the complexity of a quantum-stated problem? That’s where the idea of quantum computational complexity comes in, and if we want to understand what the latest advance of proving the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture is, that’s where we need to go.

We’ve already talked about the P complexity class of problems: problems that can be solved in deterministic polynomial time. There’s a more general class of problems that includes, but isn’t restricted to, deterministic problems: probabilistic problems. If you can write an algorithm for a problem where the computer can:

  • flip coins and make random decisions,
  • runs in polynomial time,
  • and each time you run the algorithm, gives the wrong answer to a “yes/no” question no more than one-third of the time,

you fall into the class known as BPP: bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time problems. One step up from BPP, which is to say it includes BPP but is even more general, is BQP: an algorithm that can be run on a quantum computer instead of just on a classical one.

According to Scott Aaronson, the “Aaronson” in the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, attempting to separate P from BQP is where the whole idea of the conjecture came from. If you imagine having a quantum algorithm making a certain number queries to an input string, is it possible to make a purely classical simulation that made a polynomially-scaled number of queries to that same input string, and that approximates the quantum algorithm’s success for most values of that input string? If you could, you’d demonstrate that you don’t get (very much of a) quantum advantage from using a quantum algorithm for this class of problems.

As Aaronson puts it, “It would underscore that superpolynomial quantum speedups depend on structure.” Although that specific problem was never solved by anyone, it led Aaronson, in 2008, to notice that a solution would follow from a conjecture about influences in lower-degree polynomials. Then, in 2011, Andris Ambainis was working on a related problem about whether there was a polynomial relation between randomized and quantum querying simulations for partial functions with permutation symmetries. Aaronson and Ambainis worked together to put out a now-15-year-old paper called The Need for Structure in Quantum Speedups.

Thinking back to the problem of factoring large numbers (or determining if they’re prime), a quantum computer can only “defeat” the classical computer if it needs to query the initial input number exponentially fewer times than than the classical computer does. If it’s only “polynomially” fewer times, you won’t get the necessary speedup for quantum advantage. The Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture states that if you want to determine that you don’t get the necessary speedup, it is sufficient to show that the ordinary computer can imitate the quantum computer with only a polynomial-time number of additional queries. It still takes more queries, but only “a few” more queries, and so there’s no quantum advantage there.

But was the conjecture true? It was proven true for certain special cases, and it was very recently proven (in August of 2026) that if your quantum algorithm looks at your input in a fixed number of parallel rounds, you also don’t get exponential speedups. While the AI-generated proof certainly built upon this already-substantial amount of earlier work, the authors of that August 2026 paper wrote,

“This is a huge result. It resolves a decades-old conjecture with important implications for the nature of problems that admit quantum speedups. The proof draws on and extends several lines of work in the analysis of Boolean functions and probabilistic combinatorics. Everything is brought together in a rather magical way.”

What has been a longstanding conjecture — a conjecture that was widely thought to be true — has now been proven. The impact on practical quantum computing, however, is zero. It was already generally thought that you’d need some kind of special structure to get a significant speedup from a quantum computer over a classical computer, and this has now been proven to indeed be the case. In quantum physics, quantum chemistry, and materials science, we still expect that speedup to genuinely be present.

Quite fortuitously, Scott Aaronson actually gave his own take on the proof, and he’s quite impressed. However, as he noted:

  • the proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture doesn’t kill quantum supremacy,
  • it doesn’t change how we’re going to build quantum computers,
  • it doesn’t mean that Scott himself actually understands the proof as it was presented (he notes that he’s no longer an expert on his own conjecture),
  • that it only rules out a class of quantum speedups that most people didn’t think would exist,
  • and that right now is an age where a large number of longstanding open problems in all of computer science and mathematics are falling, so it’s no surprise that this conjecture has now been proven.

The only type of quantum supremacy that’s dead is a type that would have meant quantum querying yes-or-no problems relative to random oracles, which was long conjectured to not exist anyways. No form of quantum supremacy that is actually conjectured to exist is affected by this proof!

So it’s great that we’ve proven and confirmed an expected-to-be-true conjecture, and it’s great that people with expertise are impressed at the proof itself. If we hope for quantum advantage, it’s useful to know where we should and shouldn’t be looking, and this tells us one place, for certain, where we definitely shouldn’t be looking any further. Still, all of the math and computer science (and physics) proofs that have arrived from AI have heavily built on human-made work that led us up to this point.

It makes one wonder: is AI close to reaching the limits of what it will actually be able to solve? And if the answer is no, will there be any humans around who can even understand what those next-level discoveries will mean? Only time will provide the answer to those questions.

This article AI proved a major quantum complexity conjecture. What does it mean? is featured on Big Think.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Tens of thousands of AI-built apps exposed with leaked secrets shows how AI coding changes security. (score 7)

From The Hacker News.

Of the 37,571 Grok-built apps that security company Claroc found online, 35,578 were open to anyone without a sign-in, the researchers said yesterday.

They included 24 apps built by staff at the social network X and at SpaceXSI, the company that makes the Grok AI assistant. Most of the open apps were games, landing pages, and calculators, but about 1 in 10 contained internal business or personal data.

The staff apps included a confidential onboarding plan for a new sales hire, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, and an X advertising proposal to a U.S. federal agency marked confidential. SpaceXSI, formerly known as xAI, has since taken down all 24 staff apps but not other users' apps, the researchers said.

Besides those staff apps, the open apps contained internal data from 30 other organizations the researchers could identify, across fields ranging from construction and energy to healthcare and defense. Of those, 26 have more than 1,000 employees, and 6 are Fortune 500 companies.

According to the researchers' estimate in their report, roughly 2% of the open apps contained material serious enough to rate as high or critical.

The exposed material included a hospital group's searchable list of more than 3,500 employees, an intensive care briefing on a single patient, a fire department's live shift board, and a contractor's timesheet whose code held every employee's password in plain text.

Grok can build a working app from a description typed into its chat, a feature its maker opened to every Grok plan on August 19. This chat builder shares the Grok Build name with a separate terminal coding tool, whose repository uploads were reported on July 14.

Each published app gets its own subdomain of grok.me, and its creator chooses who can open it, according to the company's launch announcement.

No app goes public until its creator clicks Publish. In the paid account the researchers used, the next step offered 3 access settings: "Anyone with the link", "Invited users" and "Only you". "Anyone with the link" was already selected.

The setting matters because an app's address does not stay secret, the researchers say. Opening an app makes the visitor's computer look up its subdomain in DNS. Passive DNS services record such lookups, and anyone with an account can search those records by pattern.

Grok suggests 4 random words as each app's name, and about half of the names the researchers found followed that pattern. Such names are hard to guess, but that does not protect an app whose name already sits in a searchable list.

ChatGPT's app builder also puts each app on its own subdomain. But when the researchers shared an app there, its access was set to "Only me" until they changed it. A ChatGPT app address found in DNS data would lead to an app that only its owner can open, they say.

The researchers found the Grok app names using common subdomain discovery methods and loaded each app's first page once, without signing in.

To see what protection Grok adds on its own, the researchers built 2 test apps with made-up data and published both with the access setting already selected, "Anyone with the link".

The first, a contact list, got a database but no sign-in. Without signing in, the researchers added a row from a private browser window, and the next visitor saw it.

The second, a customer list for a 4-person sales team, got sign-in buttons that Grok added on its own: "Continue with Google" and "Continue with X". But the code Grok wrote added each person who signed in to the team before checking whether they belonged, so the check always passed.

An uninvited Google account belonging to someone other than the owner got in, viewed every customer, edited one record, and deleted another.

The researchers ran these tests only on their own apps. They did not test whether any of the open apps they found would accept such changes.

The researchers reported their findings to SpaceXSI on Sunday through the address in its security.txt file, including 2 of the staff apps. They reported the other 22 on Monday.

By the time the researchers published yesterday, the company had not replied to their report, but it had answered a reporter's questions about the research.

As the researchers describe, the company said Grok apps stay private until their creator shares them. Publishing takes several steps, including choosing between "Only you" and "Anyone with the link," as well as a legal disclaimer. Employee accounts are set to "Only you" by default.

Even so, 24 apps built by staff at the company and at X were open to anyone, the researchers say.

With their report, the researchers had asked the company to make "Only you" the default and to add an option that limits an app to a company's own email domain.

The company's response did not state that it would contact the owners of other open apps, according to the researchers. They have started emailing the affected organizations themselves and had emailed 3 by the time they published. They withheld every app address and title from the report.

On October 18, the same researchers published Muse research showing that pages shared from Meta's Muse AI agent could be found through passive DNS. Meta disabled sharing, then announced a sharing fix on October 22 that gave shared items new addresses.

How to Check Your Organization's Grok Apps

Claroc, which sells tools to find and secure apps built with AI, recommends these checks:

  • Find out which AI app builders your staff uses. Builders such as Grok, Lovable, Replit, v0, Bolt, Base44 and Google AI Studio can be used without IT setting them up or a company account.
  • If you have access to passive DNS data, look up the builders' domains and open any results in a private browser window.
  • Make sure any Grok app with internal data is set to "Invited users" or "Only you", and that a stranger gets an error page.
  • Try to sign in with an account from outside your company. If it gets in, the app needs a list of who is allowed.
  • Check the scripts each app loads for names, email addresses and passwords, and unpublish apps that have no owner.

In the researchers' tests, setting an app to "Only you" caused it to return a 401 error to a stranger for both the page and its data, and unpublishing took an app offline within seconds.

Google News,

item.content:encoded:
Why: A breach of stored AI keys with large losses is a key management lesson. (score 7)

From The Hacker News.

AI provider keys that customers stored on Railway were stolen in an October breach and used to commit an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized spending, the platform-as-a-service provider said yesterday. It has promised to pay those charges itself when an AI provider will not refund them.

The company builds and runs apps for its customers and stores their secrets, such as API keys and database credentials, as environment variables. The attacker decrypted variables in at most 1.85% of workspaces, about 100,000, and its database queries looked for AI provider keys.

In an October 26 update, the company told customers asking about refunds for unauthorized AI spend that "Railway is unable to refund customers for spend performed with compromised API keys." It encouraged them to contact the AI providers directly and offered to escalate their requests.

According to the company's incident report, the decrypted data also included linked-account tokens for 1,852 users: BYOK agent keys and GitHub OAuth tokens. All were reset, each user was notified, and no logins to customer accounts using stolen credentials were found.

In addition to AI keys, one of the attacker's database queries matched cloud, database, and payment service credentials. The company's forensics did not show any customer databases being accessed, and there was no indication that customers' code repositories were downloaded.

The attacker also read the stored histories of 353 builds, including the variables and secrets passed to those builds.

The company's logs show which environments were exposed but not which variables, so the figure of about 100,000 workspaces is an upper limit. It emailed customers it judged to be at high risk.

Any data the attacker copied but did not decrypt can no longer be decrypted, because the credential the attacker used has been disabled, according to the company.

What Railway Customers Can Do

Refund terms differ by AI provider, according to the company's incident report:

  • AWS Bedrock: AWS's existing refund policy covers fraud, and its account teams have started refunds.
  • Google Gemini: Google's existing refund policy covers fraud, and its account teams have started refunds.
  • OpenAI: Refunds are reviewed on a case-by-case basis. Customers file a claim with OpenAI, then pass the case ID to Railway's support team.
  • SpaceXSI: Refunds are reviewed on a case-by-case basis, and customers submit their claims to the same support team.
  • Anthropic: Talks are still underway, and the platform will cover costs from breached Anthropic keys in the meantime.
  • OpenRouter: It maintains its no-refund policy in its terms of service, so the platform will cover all OpenRouter-related costs resulting from the breach.

Customers are asked to report charges they did not make through a charge report form. The form says the company "is not responsible for usage of these keys" but is investigating the theft and working with the providers.

The report does not say how the $740,000 figure was estimated or what period it covers. Neither it nor the form sets a cap or a deadline for claims, or states whether customers must pay disputed charges while a claim is under review.

The company advises customers to revoke and replace any sensitive variable stored on the platform before October 21. Keys should be revoked or rotated with the provider that issued them, since filing a charge report does not revoke a key.

It also advises removing public network access to databases, checking GitHub audit logs and which apps can access the account, and checking audit logs in registries such as Docker Hub. Most of this advice dates from the company's October disclosure and a report it published the next day.

Out of caution, the company also gave some providers every key it held for their services, so reset requests reached more than 100,000 users. A revocation notice from a provider does not by itself mean a key was exposed.

How the Railway Breach Happened

The attack began in the company's build system, according to its incident report. At 07:28 UTC on October 20, the attacker exploited a previously unknown flaw to partly escape the filesystem isolation around a build and read some files on the host virtual machine.

That gave the attacker a credential that build servers use to push finished images and reach some internal systems. The on-call engineer was paged at 13:58 UTC, about six and a half hours after the first exploit, when an alert flagged unusual calls to a registry service.

The credential was meant only for build work, but the company's internal Temporal system, which drives parts of the build process, accepted it as a trusted client. Through it, the attacker read some stored histories of other builds.

The same credential could also fetch cached snapshots of code. That gave the attacker a copy of the company's internal monorepo, the code base that many of its services deploy from. The company says the copy showed the attacker how the platform works and helped them find exploits and move quickly between systems.

After scanning that code, the attacker found a wrongly configured OIDC binding in one of the company's cloud environments. The binding is part of how its deployment system obtains short-lived cloud credentials, and at 03:26 UTC on October 21, the attacker exploited the mistake to obtain one.

With that credential, the attacker took two more from the cloud environment. One could read encrypted variables from a production database when used inside the internal network, and the other was an SSH key.

The SSH key opened a machine that runs orchestration tasks for the company's fleet. That machine stored a credential capable of decrypting customer variables, which it needed to start customer workloads.

Each environment's variables are encrypted with that environment's own key, and those keys are, in turn, encrypted by a root key stored in a cloud provider's key management service (KMS).

Between 04:07 and 05:21 UTC on October 21, the attacker pulled encrypted variables from the database, looking for names that matched AI provider keys. Using the orchestration machine's credentials with the KMS, it decrypted some of them between 04:42 and 05:14 UTC and again between 06:36 and 07:15 UTC.

The attacker was fully removed from the company's systems at 09:24 UTC that day.

Those times differ from the company's preliminary report of October 22, which dated the attack from 13:58 UTC on October 20 and placed decryption after 05:27 UTC.

Each build now runs in its own short-lived virtual machine, on top of the old isolation. Its credentials can push only one specific image to the company's registry.

Within an hour of the company patching the original escape, its own hardening team built a second exploit by changing that attack. That was one reason the company moved every user to the new build system at once.

Every weakness the attacker used is now closed, the company says. It has filed a complaint with the FBI's IC3 and is working with a specialist forensics firm whose investigation continues.

It is sharing indicators of compromise privately for now and plans to publish them once law enforcement agrees.

The company believes the stolen credentials were used by services that relay or resell access to AI providers for use in distillation. It has not established whether the attacker ran those services, nor has it named the attacker.

In their Black October analysis, Wiz researchers list this breach among incidents disclosed in October by at least nine AI developer platforms, including the earlier OpenCode breach.

Every public report describes attackers hunting for stored environment variables, especially ones that grant AI access, the researchers say. No single flaw or software dependency links the attacks.

Google News,

item.content:encoded:
Why: MCP support coming to Apple iWork apps is a notable Apple and AI automation story. (score 7)

From MacSparky.

John Voorhees has been testing the upcoming Creator Studio updates, including beta MCP support for Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. His report gives us an early look at AI agents working directly with those apps.

There are some practical details worth knowing. The app has to be open, and if you have several windows open, the agent needs to identify the one it should work on.

Keynote is getting a new interchange format, too, designed to make presentations easier for other tools to work with.

I keep beating the drum that productivity apps need to adapt for use with agentic AI going forward, and I’m glad to see the iWork team is getting on board.

I write about getting more from your Apple gear. If this was useful, go deeper in the Labs or grab the weekly newsletter.

item.title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
item.author: Krebs on Security
item.description:
Why: Microsoft's November Patch Tuesday fixes nearly 1,100 flaws, a record-scale drop a Microsoft security PM should know about. (score 8)

From Krebs on Security. Also covered by Zero Day Initiative - Blog.

Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month's Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws -- including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook -- and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.
item.content:encoded:
Why: Microsoft's November Patch Tuesday fixes nearly 1,100 flaws, a record-scale drop a Microsoft security PM should know about. (score 8)

From Krebs on Security. Also covered by Zero Day Initiative - Blog.

Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues applying this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Gruber highlights Gary Marcus's skeptical case on the economics behind Anthropic's IPO. (score 7)

From Daring Fireball.

Gary Marcus:

When a business needs exponentially increasing amounts of capital to make modest increases in quality in an intensely competitive market and still owes far more money than it has ever made, there is a serious problem.

I continue to believe that there is no moat in AI models. None. But the entire premise of Anthropic’s IPO is that they have an enormous gulf of a moat.

I would not be shocked to see Anthropic go out of business. Nor would I be shocked if the IPO fails. WeWork tried to IPO, 3 times, and didn’t make it.

I would be surprised if Anthropic does not go out of business. Most cults implode, and Anthropic doesn’t even hide that they’re a cult. And I just don’t see how the math works. Scientology is a long-running cult, but Scientology hasn’t committed $900 billion in spending over the next few years.

(Marcus’s post is on his Substack blog, which, annoyingly, requires you to be logged into a Substack account and to “subscribe”, even though it’s ostensibly a free post. What a rotten oppressive turd of a blogging platform Substack is. Just in case your Substack account isn’t working, here’s a PDF archive.)

Link: garymarcus.substack.com/p/just-say-no-to-anthropics-ipo?r…

item.content:encoded:
Why: Six Colors argues Apple's HomeView should be a focused home hub, not another app store. (score 7)

From Six Colors.

This may sound like an odd request coming from a guy whose to-do list includes filing a weekly App Report highlighting interesting macOS and iOS offerings, but I really hope Apple keeps a tight lid on the apps that can appear on its HomeView smart display. I’d even take that wish one step further to implore app makers not to flood the zone with HomeView-based offerings if there ever comes a day that Apple does open up development for its latest device.

This is not me hoping for less work in the future due to laziness, though Lord knows, I am that. Rather, it’s a recognition of the fact that, as showcased by Apple, the HomeView seems to serve a very specific purpose and turning it into a device that can run every app under the sun like the iPhone and iPad before it might lessen its effectiveness.

The HomeView needs to act as a hub when you need it to be and stay out of the way the rest of the time. And loading it up with too many apps might make it more difficult for the HomeView to recede into the background.

From what I’ve seen of HomeView during its October debut, Apple designed this $299 hub as a way to control your smarthome devices while also taking care of a few other tasks, whether that’s listening to music, checking out recipes, staying up to date on your messages or what have you. That’s true whether we’re talking about the table-top model with its adjustable Liquid Retina display or the version of HomeView that you mount on the wall. In either case, the guiding principle of HomeView appears to be simplicity.

What HomeView doesn’t appear to be is a device that demands to be at the center of your life, even if “hub” is part of the description. You’re already carrying around a device that keeps you constantly connected in the form of an iPhone, and when you need a big screen for more intensive work, you can turn to a Mac or even an iPad. In contrast, the HomeView seems like it’s designed for very specific purposes and not much else.

The app situation on the initial model arriving in stores on November 13 reflects that. Apple lists 15 included apps on board the HomeView, and apart from Intercom — a HomeView-specific app that lets you make audio announcements throughout the home to connected speakers — they’re going to be familiar offerings to anyone who’s used an Apple device.

There’s the Home app, of course, for controlling smart devices from a central location, and Apple includes a few other familiar faces for managing your daily life. Apps like Calendar, Reminders and Weather give you an overview of your day. Safari lets you browse the web from your HomeView, with a special mode for displaying recipes if you’ve got the device set up in a kitchen. Music and Podcasts let you stream entertainment while you’re going about your business, and you can connect to TV, Audiobooks and a handful of other options on your iPhone for additional entertainment resources. And there’s FaceTime for video chats — ideal for the HomeView since you don’t have to hold the device and talk like you would on an iPhone or iPad.

Save for a workaround for audio and video apps that support CarPlay, you can’t install apps on your HomeView. There’s also no App Store, suggesting that Apple thinks of this device as a closed shop, at least out of the gate.

Of course, the iPhone took the same approach initially. It’s hard to remember after two decades of “There’s an app for that” marketing, but the phone Steve Jobs showed off back in 2007 had 15 apps, and that was that. It took a year for Apple to open up the iPhone for third-party apps, and developers were quick to make up for lost time.

Could a similar scenario play out with the HomeView? Certainly, it’s possible. If you’re already using your home hub to look up recipes, why not add a calorie-counting or meal-planning app? You can access your daily schedule and your to-dos, so why not add your health data as well, with maybe some exercise apps thrown in for good measure? Oh, and the HomeView supports entertainment apps, you say? Well, nothing’s more entertaining than games, all the games, oh so many games.

That’s the sort of mission creep I think Apple must avoid with the HomeView. Some apps for managing your life make sense, so long as they’re consistent with the idea of a central hub that you’re checking when it’s convenient. But if you keep expanding that functionality to an ever-increasing array of apps, the HomeView becomes just another screen you wind up staring at, no different from an iPhone or iPad or what have you. And perhaps paradoxically, the need for a device like a HomeView dissipates as its functionality expands.

So my plea for the HomeView — to Apple, to app makers, to anyone who will listen really — is to think long and hard about expanding the home hub’s ability to add apps. Take it from someone who ekes out a living reviewing these sorts of things: Sometimes less is more.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Snell points to Hackett's deep history of Virginia Tech's Mac-based supercomputers. (score 7)

From Six Colors.

by Jason Snell

The Mac-based Virginia Tech supercomputers

Stephen Hackett has a great, in-depth history of that time Virginia Tech built one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers out of Macs—twice:

Tech tore down the Power Mac version of System X in January 2004 and rebuilt it with Xserve G5s that summer. ECC memory was a big part of the reason. As the school put it: “We needed to upgrade the system to something with error correcting code (ECC) RAM. The Power Macs did not support it and the XServes were coming.”

The new array was made up of 1,100 dual 2.3 GHz Xserve G5 servers and six Xserve RAIDs. Those 2.3 GHz machines were custom-built by Apple for Virginia Tech; the public wouldn’t be able to buy one until January 2005. Each one had 4 GB of that sweet, sweet ECC RAM and an 80 GB Serial ATA drive.

I love the extra mile Stephen went with the research on this one. Featuring some never-before-seen photos!

item.content:encoded:
Why: A Git flaw let malicious repos run code during recursive clones, a supply chain risk every engineer touches. (score 7)

From The Hacker News.

A flaw in Git can let a malicious repository run an attacker's code on a computer that clones it recursively, together with its submodules. The Git project fixed it this week in Git 2.56.1, with matching fixes for the 2.50 through 2.55 series in 2.50.2, 2.51.3, 2.52.1, 2.53.1, 2.54.1 and 2.55.1.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111760, is an integer truncation in how Git handles its index. An extremely long path in a repository can pass Git's safety check, but Git then writes it to disk under a shorter name that an attacker can set to .git.

This lets an attacker replace a submodule's .git file with a symbolic link to a folder holding malicious hooks or configuration. Hooks are programs Git runs at set points, so once Git uses that folder, the attacker's code can run.

Submodules matter here because Git refuses to replace a .git folder with a symbolic link, but in a freshly cloned submodule, .git is a file.

The fixed versions, listed in the Git project's release announcement, refuse such extremely long paths before their length can be cut short.

GitHub, which ships Git in its own tools, explained the fixes in a detailed write-up. It advises installing a fixed version from your operating system or Git distributor, and updating any app that ships its own copy of Git.

The company has already applied the fixes to github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud. For GitHub Enterprise Server, they are in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9 and 3.22.4.

Fixed versions of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app are being prepared. GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also get the fixed Git.

Git for Windows had not released a version based on Git 2.56.1 as of Tuesday at 19:09 UTC, a check of its release tags by The Hacker News found.

Until a fixed version is installed, GitHub suggests these steps, which do not replace the fixes:

  • Clone only from servers you trust.
  • Do not recursively clone repositories you do not trust.
  • Do not merge content or tags you do not trust.
  • Do not process binary patches or fast-import streams from sources you do not trust.

The Git releases also fix five other flaws:

  • CVE-2026-113408: When someone clones an empty repository over Git protocol v2, a malicious server can send a branch name that contains path traversal. With the files reference backend, a later update to that branch can then write outside Git's reference folder.
  • CVE-2026-114467: Merging a tag that carries more than two GPG signatures corrupts Git's stack memory and can cause a denial of service. Hosting services that run such merges for users may also be affected.
  • CVE-2026-114469: A binary patch that expands to a very large size can get past Git's patch size limit of about 1 GiB and crash Git with an out-of-bounds read.
  • CVE-2026-105437: A very large merge, with many conflicts and a large conflict-marker-size attribute, can make Git write past the end of a buffer that is too small, corrupting heap memory.
  • CVE-2026-114466: Three git fast-import features, rewrite-submodules-from, rewrite-submodules-to and export-pack-edges, could be used to read arbitrary files or to create files and add data to them. Git now rejects them in an input stream unless --allow-unsafe-features is set.

GitLab, which assigned CVE-2026-105437, said code-hosting servers are most likely to be targeted through git merge-tree. A server may run that command to check whether a pull or merge request can be merged.

The conflict-marker-size attribute can be set in a .gitattributes file committed to a repository. If a server reads attributes from the repository, any user who can push branches and open a pull or merge request can trigger the flaw.

As a workaround for this flaw, servers that cannot upgrade yet can add conflict-marker-size=7 to each repository's info/attributes file, or turn off those merge checks for untrusted repositories.

Google News,
