item.content:encoded:
Why: Seth Godin on why anyone can now be the one who starts something. (score 7)

From Seth's Blog.

The cultural impresario has always had leverage.

Invest time and money and put on a show. Start a cable network, a book publishing company or become a concert promoter. You’re the gatekeeper, an adjudicator of status, a person who can transform people’s lives simply by amplifying and spreading ideas and allowing art to reach its audience.

Time and money were apparently the gating factors. It takes a while to turn a profit, and it’s uncertain and hard work.

Except…

New platforms and tools remove both time and money as barriers.

Penn and Teller needed their fame and the CW network to launch their cable show Fool Us. But now, anyone can start a competitor on YouTube in a weekend.

A radio pundit needed to spend years to build a syndicated network of terrestrial stations, but now you can start a podcast, in your basement, for free. In a weekend.

Gallerists don’t need galleries, and you don’t even need a building to coordinate a foster-home-based pet shelter.

So what’s the impediment?

I’m guessing that if you got the call today, you could put together your ideas for a book, or five minutes of standup or even the software you’d code.

But we don’t need the specific call. We’ve all been called.

The barrier is simple: fear. The fear of beginning and of sticking with it. The fear of succeeding (or failing). The fear of impostor syndrome. And the fear of going forward without a guarantee.

So let’s call it that. Fear is real, but fear might not be rational.

Begin.

item.title: Why are we all worked up about atomicity when applying hot-patches if we can just suspend all the threads?
item.author: The Old New Thing
item.description:
Why: Raymond Chen on why hot-patching needs atomicity, a classic Windows engineering lesson. (score 7)

From The Old New Thing.

Suspending all the threads stops the threads that are there now, those are not the only possible sources of change. The post Why are we all worked up about atomicity when applying hot-patches if we can just suspend all the threads? appeared first on The Old New Thing .
item.content:encoded:
Why: Raymond Chen on why hot-patching needs atomicity, a classic Windows engineering lesson. (score 7)

From The Old New Thing.

I noted that one of the concerns of the Windows hot-patching system is that the patch can be activated atomically. But why does it need to be atomic? Can’t just suspend all the threads of the process (except for the one doing the patching)? That way, nobody else can be executing a half-installed patch.

For processors with variable-length instructions (looking at you, x86), the patched instruction cannot be shorter than its replacement. This applies even if you can suspend all the threads of the process, because you might suspend a thread just as it’s about to execute bytes from what would be the second of half of the replacement instruction.

instruction
pointer
    ↓
original XX YY
 
patch AA BB

If you were unlucky and froze the thread after it executed the XX instruction and was about to execute the YY instruction, and then replaced both bytes with a two-byte instruction AA BB, then when the thread resumes, it will execute BB as if it were the start of a new instruction.

Okay fine, so we’ll make sure that the original instruction is at least as big as the replacement instruction, so that a frozen thread is never caught in the middle of the replacement instruction. But assuming we do that, can’t we just suspend all the threads, and then patch at will without having to worry about atomicity?

While it’s true that you suspended all the threads in the process, that doesn’t prevent new threads from being created in the process by a function like Create­Remote­Thread. The caller of Create­Remote­Thread can specify whether the new thread is suspended or not, and if it chooses non-suspended (or if it chose suspended and then decided to resume it), you now have a live thread running in the process while you are busy trying to patch it.

Atomicity is important so that you don’t accidentally patch code while an injected thread happens to be running it.

Bonus chatter: Now, atomicity is still not bulletproof, because even if you manage to suspend all the threads, and prevent new ones from being injected, you still have the case where somebody calls Write­Process­Memory to modify the bytes of the process while everything in it is suspended.

And we saw earlier that Write­Process­Memory is not atomic, so it’s possible that a two-byte Write­Process­Memory writes the first byte, and then you do your atomic update of both bytes, and then the Write­Process­Memory finishes by writing the second byte, leaving a mishmash of your patch and the rogue one.

On the other hand, anybody who was using Write­Process­Memory to do code patching was already broken because of this lack of atomicity, so we are not introducing a new problem.

Furthermore, since the hot-patching space is reserved for Windows Update, an outsider that uses Write­Process­Memory to apply a hot-patch from another process is already breaking the rules. At this point Windows Update says, “Look, I can’t protect myself from this, and you’re in double-unsupported territory by the time we got here, so whatever happens is your problem.”

The post Why are we all worked up about atomicity when applying hot-patches if we can just suspend all the threads? appeared first on The Old New Thing.

That's according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation […]
item.content:encoded:
Why: Report that AI is speeding up AI development itself, a big shift in how software is built. (score 7)

From The Verge.

Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company’s models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down.

Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers

AI is dramatically speeding up Anthropic’s research, even as the company calls for slowing down AI development.

Inside Anthropic Headquarters As It’s Testing A Different Version Of Leadership

Inside Anthropic Headquarters As It’s Testing A Different Version Of Leadership

That’s according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development. The probe is separate from a program offering safety researchers “employee-like” access to systems in the wake of high-profile hacking incidents over the summer.

The findings offer some of the clearest evidence yet of AI accelerating its own development, raising questions about how quickly the technology could advance toward a future in which AI systems can improve themselves with little or no human involvement. They also come at a pivotal time for Anthropic, which is preparing to go public even as its CEO, Dario Amodei, has publicly called for labs to pump the brakes on AI development.

But while the report offers a rare glimpse into the inner workings of the world’s leading AI labs, what it leaves out is just as revealing. Anthropic was permitted to redact portions of the final report as part of its agreement with METR, and it appears to have exercised that power liberally, raising questions about how much the public really knows about the pace — and risks — of frontier AI development.

Here are some of the biggest takeaways.

AI is dramatically accelerating Anthropic’s research and development

One of METR’s most noteworthy findings is that Anthropic’s AI models are improving roughly twice as quickly as they were a year ago, with benchmark scores suggesting “that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.” Crucially, METR’s researchers said they “are confident” that the acceleration was not simply due to scaling up the computing power used to train the models, which historically has been a major driver of AI progress.

Instead, the researchers said that the majority of the acceleration as of October “is due to AI,” with its contribution growing over time. That finding was supported by informal Slack polls and interviews with Anthropic employees, which pointed to sizable productivity gains. METR wrote that employees using Anthropic’s most capable internal model on average self-reported being around 12 times as productive at their respective work as they would have been without AI assistance, around double what staff had reported just a few months earlier while using Mythos 5.

METR’s report includes this graphic showing Anthropic employees’ responses to Slack polls about AI speeding up their work.

For now, much of that acceleration appears to be coming from AI assisting human researchers, rather than AI working independently, though METR warned that “there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.” Notably, the researchers said they found no clear signs of diminishing returns or observable bottlenecks that could prevent “even faster acceleration.”

Three of Anthropic’s newest AI models remain under wraps

Anthropic’s researchers are using more advanced AI models than the rest of us, with a lot of the acceleration and productivity gains described by METR attributable to unreleased internal models.

Over the past six months, Anthropic has finished training three models it has yet to release, according to METR. The pace of development is swift, with the models — codenamed Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4 — completing training in July, August-September, and September-October, respectively. METR also identified an unreleased model dating back to 2022, called Unreleased 2022. “These are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames,” the researchers wrote.

Anthropic is keeping key information secret

Anthropic gave METR access to a host of non-public information, including confidential research, model performance data, and employee interviews as part of the research process. It had no obligation to do so and by METR’s own admission, the AI lab “shared more information than was initially scoped for this project, surpassing our expectations.” This is commendable, but it is worth noting that Anthropic did not grant researchers unrestricted access, nor the kind of “employee-like” access it has promised other METR safety researchers as part of a separate program announced last month. It is an important distinction, given the reputational benefits companies can gain from independent assessments, even when they come with significant restrictions.

And there were significant restrictions. Anthropic had the power to redact information from METR’s final report — and it used that power extensively. “We submitted a ~100-page full report on our assessment to Anthropic. For the public version, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative,” METR wrote on X.

METR reiterated those concerns throughout the report, highlighting other limitations on its access. “Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied.”

METR repeatedly stressed the impact Anthropic’s redaction decisions had on its ability to communicate its findings and for others to assess what’s going on at the company. It noted that much of the redacted evidence could have “multiple plausible interpretations,” making it difficult for the public to assess its findings, understand the uncertainties surrounding them, and judge the evidence themselves. “As a consequence [of the redactions], the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here,” the report said.

In the report, METR said Anthropic justified the redactions on the grounds that releasing the information could benefit its rivals. However, METR said “most of the redacted information was very high-level,” even though it said it was not in position to comment whether redactions were justified commercially or not.

“We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work,” Anthropic cofounder Sam McCandlish acknowledged in a lengthy post on X responding to METR’s findings. “But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster,” he said, adding that doing so would make the risks METR is concerned about “worse.”

McCandlish said that it’s a trade-off, but maintained Anthropic had made the “right call” in deciding to redact the information. He said the company plans to publish its own report on the speed of AI progress “in the coming weeks,” as well as new steps it’s taking to strengthen safety.

Anthropic is accelerating the very technology it warns is dangerous and faster than many expected

The publication of METR’s report has provoked a fierce backlash among AI safety researchers and commentators, largely centered on an apparent contradiction at the heart of Anthropic’s approach to AI: The company has been one of the most outspoken advocates for safety and responsible development, yet the report suggests it is helping accelerate the technology toward a threshold many consider dangerous, while seemingly failing to live up to its own commitments to transparency and accountability.

For some, the findings suggest that even many of the field’s most aggressive predictions about AI progress may be too conservative. They indicate that recursive self-improvement — AI systems that can autonomously develop increasingly powerful successor systems without human intervention, potentially accelerating development dramatically — may be closer than previously thought, raising concerns about whether existing safety measures can keep pace. While METR’s report only covers Anthropic, OpenAI said in September that it is “making strong progress” toward building an AI researcher that can “further progress on deep learning and alignment” by March 2028.

The report provides evidence about just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development

Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which conducts AI safety testing for several leading AI labs, told The Verge the report suggests a pace of AI-enabled research and development even faster than what was forecast in AI 2027, an influential scenario that envisions a key breakthrough toward self-improvement in early 2027. He said the report has attracted so much attention because it provides evidence about something that has been very hard to pin down: Just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development.

Hobbhahn said the findings were broadly in line with what many in the field had expected, perhaps a little faster. Alan Chan, a senior research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI, told The Verge that the findings should prompt skeptics to reconsider their stance on AI accelerating AI development, and possibly shorten their timelines to when we will have systems that can fully automate tasks like software engineering.

On X, other researchers commented on the rate of acceleration and its implications for AI development. Sydney Von Arx, founder and CEO of AI safety organization The Nightingale Collective and a former METR researcher, also compared the findings to AI 2027’s timeline. Ryan Greenblatt, a METR researcher formerly of AI safety organization Redwood Research and one of three external researchers permitted to investigate OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face, said he “was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026.”

Frustration is mounting over Anthropic’s approach to safety

Beyond highlighting the speed of AI development, the report has also fueled a growing sense of frustration over Anthropic’s role in driving that progress. The company has been one of the most vocal proponents of responsible AI development — and no stranger to calling for others to slow down — yet appears to be racing ahead itself. This report only builds on already heightened tensions from its IPO prospectus and future plans released last month.

Anthropic’s decision to heavily redact the report, citing grounds that revealing more could help its rivals accelerate their own development, has fueled accusations of hypocrisy. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who now runs the AI Futures Project, which published AI 2027, accused Anthropic of “recklessly gambling with our lives,” adding that “it is pretty rich” of the company to cite others going faster as a reason to redact information when it does “not appear to be slowing down much at all.”

Anthropic declined to answer The Verge’s questions about the report and ensuing criticism, instead directing us to McCandlish’s post.

The redactions have also renewed calls for greater transparency and independent oversight of frontier AI labs, which grew to new heights earlier this year following a spate of incidents involving rogue AI agents. Brianna Rosen, research director for frontier security at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, told The Verge that it was concerning that companies, not governments, were effectively calling the shots on automating AI research. “For democratic oversight to work, independent evaluators need the freedom to explain why they reached their conclusions, governments need to assess the evidence themselves, and the public has to trust this process,” Rosen said. “The report was not sufficiently transparent about the evidence.”

Pressure is building for more transparency from AI labs

Hobbhahn echoed Rosen’s concerns, saying that much of the reaction to the report stems from the apparent gap between Anthropic’s public safety stance and its actions. He pointed to the company’s decision to cancel part of the assessment designed to evaluate how much compute it allocates to safety work versus improving capabilities. METR said the company said “this was due to wanting to keep the engagement focused on risk assessment for the time being, and that it would revisit compute allocation verification later on.”

For Hobbhahn, the episode underscores the need for independent safety researchers to be embedded more deeply within AI labs, with significant access to internal systems and evidence. While his organization stands to benefit from such arrangements — Apollo is taking steps toward becoming an embedded evaluator at frontier labs — he is far from alone in calling for stronger oversight of AI development.

Others have called for more direct action. In a direct response to the report, New York state Assemblyman Alex Bores, a key figure shaping the Democrats’ AI agenda, called on Congress to “ban RSI, this year if possible.” With the blue wave of Democrats — many of whom campaigned against AI companies — taking office soon, the prospect of tougher restrictions is a very real possibility.

And with AI research showing little sign of slowing down, the pressure is set to intensify. Hobbhahn said he had another takeaway from the report, too: “Brace for craziness,” he said. “It is going to go very fast,” likely way too fast for society or politics to keep up.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Gruber's take on Apple's new touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro, the week's biggest Apple story. (score 9)

From Daring Fireball.

I’m not cut out for Los Angeles.

It’s hard not to love the place, though. The weather is absurd. The people in LA, by and large, don’t believe in bad weather. It’s like a legend to them, like hearing about the Irish Potato Famine.

Angelenos are friendly and good looking. The food is good and varied. But you really do need to drive everywhere. Trips from any one part of the city to another invariably require time not just in a car but on a freeway. What is oft-described as LA’s sprawl, I would describe as a layout and geographic scale that is more like that of a small, densely populated nation than of a mere city. LA’s palpable vastness is incredible, in a wholly different sense than, say, Manhattan’s. I love to visit. I would never want to stay.

The greater San Francisco Bay Area, I don’t feel that way about. The weather there, too, is certainly nicer than back east, but it’s not implausibly nice. San Francisco is a walkable city and can punish you with its weather at certain times of the year. I’m not at all religious but I was raised in a Catholic family, and one way that’s stuck with me is that I innately believe we deserve some stretches of bad weather. That it’s good for us to suffer to some extent, like physical exercise and toiling at our jobs. That’s a stupid thing to believe, I know, but I believe it. We all believe some stupid things.

Los Angeles is an unusual place for Apple to hold a media event. They hold two big annual events on campus at Apple Park in Cupertino each year: WWDC in June, and the iPhone (and friends) event in September. Back in the old days, they held their major keynotes in San Francisco. I liked the old events in San Francisco better, if only because I enjoyed staying a few days in vibrant, gritty San Francisco better than the somnolent, sterile South Bay. But I think the events were more interesting too. Not better per se, but just more interesting. Less polished. More unique. Every inch of the Steve Jobs Theater was designed and crafted to host events like the annual iPhone introductions. It is an architectural marvel. But its perfection is off-putting. It somehow doesn’t quite feel realistic, even when you’re right there.

In its San Francisco events of yore, Apple experimented. The Macworld Expo and WWDC keynotes in Moscone North had an unavoidable sameness to them. But Apple held other events in other places in the 2010s, like the small Yerba Buena Theater across the street from Moscone, and the cavernous Bill Graham Civic Auditorium, which was built in 1915 and looks, feels, and smells like it. The room Apple used for its post-keynote hands-on area at Yerba Buena was always a little claustrophobic and very dark. This photo I took after the introduction of the original iPad in 2010 captures the feel of that room during those events.

A few years later, they held an event there in October 2013 and solved — or at least improved — the problem by knocking a hole in the wall to allow in some sunlight and fresh air. Here’s a picture from the hands-on area at that event, showing Tim Cook (Katie Cotton at his side, as ever) chatting with Ed Baig (then at USA Today, still on the beat today at AARP). You can see the open air over Cook’s shoulder.

After that event wound down, I grabbed lunch nearby, and then walked back through the plaza next to the theater. I don’t remember why. Best guess is that it was simply on the path back to my hotel. Apple already had a crew taking apart the entrance they’d added to the theater. Katie Cotton was outside, supervising. I stopped to chat. This was around 2:20pm, a little over four hours after the keynote and probably only 90 minutes after they’d politely escorted the last of us from the hands-on area inside. I didn’t write notes or record the chat, which would have been weird, but as best I recall, the conversation started with my saying something like “Man, you guys don’t waste any time, do you?” Cotton told me that while Apple loved the Yerba Buena venue, they were always bothered by the hands-on area being closed off and dark. I said that yes, it was previously a dank hellhole, and she laughed. She always seemed to genuinely enjoy my sarcasm. Apple, she explained, had inquired about options for opening that wall. Yerba Buena told them, sure, they could do whatever they wanted so long as they restored it after the event, but it would cost a small fortune. But to Apple the price was negligible, and they accepted the offer immediately and commenced with plans for how to do it.1 Cotton liked how it turned out, and I told her I agreed. It made for a noticeably nicer space.

My column about that October 2013 event began thus:

There is a certain sameness to almost every Apple event. A pattern, a formula, a structure, a rhythm and pacing. Does this make them boring? In some ways, certainly, insofar as the only thing we don’t know is what they’re going to say, as opposed to how they’re going to say it. (And even then, we often have a pretty good idea what they’re going to announce, too.)

And I went on to quote from — and then disagree with — then-NYT tech columnist Nick Bilton’s griping that Apple’s keynotes lacked “wow” and had grown stale. (Bilton is now leading failson David Ellison’s team of dipshit weasels who are sinking 60 Minutes, the crown jewel of CBS News.)

Somehow, here we are 13 years later (alas, not all of us), and there are still complaints about the repetitive sameness of Apple’s events. Yet Apple’s events these days don’t resemble that event from 2013 at all. Change comes slowly but it always comes.

I enjoyed last week’s “Pro and Tell” event more than any in recent memory. I enjoyed the venue — both the unique building and the city. I enjoyed the format. But most of all I loved the subject: the Mac.

The building is best known as CBS Columbia Square, opened in 1937 as the West Coast headquarters for CBS. The color of the event was blue — matching the default wallpaper for the new MacBook Pros with PROLED XDR displays. Blue carpet covered the sidewalk leading into the entrance. After walking up the carpet, checking in outside, and donning my press lanyard, the magnetometer dinged me, and I was pulled aside and politely but brusquely asked to put my briefcase on the (carpeted) ground, and wait for a busy police dog to take a smell at it. I presume the dog was sniffing for weapons, not drugs, but either way my bag passed muster. Inside, just past the lobby, Apple had created a rather spacious theater, with a large screen and stage. There were blue padded bench seats along the outside walls, but the primary center area of the space was for standing. From the floor to the room’s high ceiling, the walls were blue.

Behind the theater was a large area with coffee, water, and small breakfast treats. Invited guests — primarily tech journalists and social media creators — mingled and sipped. I checked my laptop bag, and carried only my notebook and phone for the morning. Apple PR reps were, as ever, present but never overpresent. Conversation touched upon the expected but as yet unknown touch-enabled MacBook Pros. Word spread that Steven Levy, the undisputed dean of the Apple press corps, had landed an exclusive first look for Wired. (Levy, ever the pro, and a delightful raconteur, confirmed only that, yes, he had the exclusive, but he offered not a word regarding its content before his agreed-upon embargo. His wry smile, though, betrayed that he was happy with what Apple was about to unveil.) Much of the pre-event chatter, however, was dominated by discussion about the iPhone Duo. A rather remarkable number of attendees had Duos in hand — many of them still in the midst of reviewing it, but others professed to having already gone all-in on it. To each their own; there’s no accounting for taste.

Shortly before 10am, word spread that it was time to pack into the theater. I squeezed in close to the stage. Why not? Steve Jobs, I noted, never took the stage quite on time. He was seldom more than two or three minutes late, but he was always at least two or three minutes late. Rock stars don’t take the stage on time. Tim Cook, on the other hand, was never late. A minute early, sometimes; a minute late, never. You could set your watch to 10:00 by listening for his “Good morning!”

John Ternus took the stage at 10:00.

He spoke briefly. Just a few minutes recapping Apple’s week of announcements. The new OLED iPad Mini, the new M6 MacBook Pro, the updates to Creator Studio. He spoke naturally and comfortably, and seemingly extemporaneously. He looks like he smells like Apple Park. He’s a cool guy. And he knows that Tim Cook handed him a killer lineup of new products to introduce over his first two months as CEO. Every one of Apple’s major platforms is in a good-to-great place. His on-stage remarks culminated with the introduction of the truly new MacBook Pros: “That’s why we’re here today — to mark another huge moment for MacBook Pro, and for the Mac itself.” When Ternus then announced, a moment later, “And yes, for the very first time, we are bringing touch to the Mac”, the audience erupted in gasps and cheers — a reminder that for as much as many of us know before Apple makes these announcements, a lot of the people in attendance do not even know who Mark Gurman is. A lot of the people in the room were genuinely shocked and surprised.

Apple paid a lot of money to put a fantastically bright screen behind Ternus, and they used that screen to show this two-minute “If you give a Mac an OLED” intro video. The first mention of touchscreen support, in that video, comes a full third of the way in.

Ternus teased the return of the glowing back-of-the-display Apple logo in a tweet that morning. On stage he made it official: “The logo is back.” I love the way he phrased that. Not “the glowing logo is back”. Just “the logo is back” — like it might as well not have been there in the unilluminated years since 2016. Fuck yeah.

The show in the theater was short and sweet. We shuttled off to the hands-on area by 10:15, if not sooner. The format of the event — or “experience”, as Apple calls these — mirrored that of the MacBook Neo experience in New York back in March. Brief welcoming remarks from Ternus, a crisp short video presented to a standing room of invited media guests, and then, boom, a scramble off to an expansive hands-on area. Apple didn’t stream Ternus’s live-on-stage remarks to the world back in March, and they chose not to again last week. They should. These aren’t live keynote events, but they are live events. I’m glad I’ve gotten to see them in person, but I wish everyone could see them online. They are good. Good things should be shown. Apple is run by people. Seeing the company’s CEO live on stage is a rare glimpse behind the aluminum and glass facade.

One is an anomaly. Two is a pattern. The Neo event (err, experience) back in March was like no other. This “Pro and Tell” MacBook Pro event was a lot like the Neo one. The Neo one didn’t get a punny title though — just a simple “You’re Invited” on the email invitation (although the decoration of the Apple logo hinted at the Neo’s signature citrus colorway). The Columbia Square building in Los Angeles is large, but it’s nowhere near as spacious as the empty warehouse in Chelsea where Apple held the Neo event. There seemingly were more invitees at last week’s event in LA too. In New York back in March, there was room to mingle. I snapped this fun photo of Jason Snell chatting with Phil Schiller, Greg Joswiak, and then-still-SVP-of-hardware John Ternus. Even setting aside Ternus’s subsequent promotion to CEO and levelling up in celebrity, that chat couldn’t have happened in the hands-on area of this event. There were too many people and too little space.

In the scramble after leaving the theater area, Apple reps were gladly informing attendees that there were two separate hands-on areas, and that “the one in the back” might be less crowded. It wasn’t. Both areas were tightly packed. They were tight tube-like hallways, with black walls, good lighting, and Apple Store-like tables upon which were arrayed the new MacBook Pros. Silver and space black; 14- and 16-inch; nano-texture and glossy. Some of the tables featured Apple’s speed-bumped M6 MacBook Pros, the enclosures for which are nearly indistinguishable from the machines everyone really wanted to see — the PROLED XDR M5 Pro and M5 Max models. I saw several attendees poking and sliding their fingers on the screens of those M6 models, to no avail, until someone gently told them “These are just the other new MacBook Pros.”

Packed shoulder-to-shoulder in a confined space with low ceilings, jostling for hands-on time with the PROLED XDR models, the temperatures — both atmospheric and emotional — got uncomfortably warm. It also became clear that some of the attendees chose not to shower that morning. The scene brought to mind the pungent imagery of the “coach” cars in Bong Joon-ho’s Snowpiercer.

The Steve Jobs Theater, this was not.

But that’s not a complaint. This was different and different is good. It was a unique event in a unique venue. That’s good for Apple and good for those of us with the fortune to be invited to attend these things. Events at Steve Jobs Theater are held the SJT way. Apple adjusts and tweaks them, but the space defines them. An altogether new venue, whose ground floor Apple seemingly built out from scratch for this event, requires thinking about everything. And Apple’s thoughts are revealing. What I took away from the hands-on at this event is that Apple wanted us to get close to these MacBooks. To really look at them and appreciate them. No, they’re not radically different. They’re subtly different. But subtly different in very significant ways. That’s not exciting but it’s correct. The old MacBook Pros (including the new M6 model) were, by far, the best professional laptops ever made. The new ones are just better.

I like the hands-on scrums. There’s an energy to them you can use to gauge interest. When the products are genuinely exciting there’s a buzz that can’t be faked. People were fucking excited by these new MacBook Pros, and rightly so. These are the machines many of the people in attendance use themselves for their own work — our own work — all day, every day. The new tandem OLED displays are quite literally brilliant. You can see the difference even when they’re not side-by-side with the old mini-LEDs. When they are side-by-side, the old displays look washed. The new ones look wow.

And the “hands-on” aspect came into literal play two ways. First, yes, you can tap, swipe, and pinch the displays. Some people cared about that. A lot of others in the room, including yours truly, not so much. But even those of us who were ambivalent, at best, about touch coming to the Mac had reason to rejoice upon seeing Apple’s implementation: Apple added touchscreen support to MacOS the right way. Touch is decidedly secondary on MacOS. The density of the UI doesn’t change at all when you’re using a mouse pointer, and it only changes slightly to create larger tap targets when you touch the screen. This is the way. I would have bet that Apple would do it this way, but every bet is uncertain. And though the likelihood was low the stakes were high — a completely touch-first reimagining of the MacOS user interface would have been a devastating blow to an irreplaceable platform.

Second, the weight reduction Apple was able to achieve with these machines is astonishing. The 14-inch models weigh a full half pound less. The 16-inch models weigh 0.7 pounds less. Almost three-quarters of a pound! I saw numerous attendees picking up the hands-on demo machines to compare them to the personal MacBook Pros they were lugging around the event in their backpacks. Eureka after eureka. These are massive reductions in weight without — claims Apple — any decrease in sustained performance or battery life.

Next up, for some of us, were product briefings. I saw a disassembled PROLED XDR display panel. Five layers (I think?), each of them impossibly thin. A friend who was in another briefing group said the front panel cover glass shattered in the hands of one writer when it was passed around for examination. In my group — which might have been after that one — we didn’t get to touch anything.

Putting OLED into a laptop doesn’t magically make it good. Apple had a side-by-side comparison with a Lenovo Yoga 9 Whatever with an OLED display. The colors on that display were slightly greenish when viewed head-on, and garishly green when viewed off-angle. The colors on Apple’s PROLED XDR look remarkably good from any angle. Most surprising to me was Windows 11’s bizarrely clunky support for HDR images. When you open an HDR image, it displays as SDR, then you wait like 5–10 seconds for the display to “warm up” and only then does it show it in HDR — and when it does, the colors look bad. Getting a brief taste of “modern” Windows feels like visiting Cuba or something.

In the not-for-attribution Q&A after the briefing, I asked about the fact that the original glowing Apple logo in MacBooks — and PowerBooks — was a byproduct of the fact that the displays were backlit. There was a bright light sealed up inside the back of those display panels, and someone at Apple had the idea that if they just cut out the Apple logo on the back and fit it with translucent plastic, it would glow. Steve Jobs loved the idea and the rest is history. Every Mac laptop from 1999 through 2016 had a logo that glowed. Photos like this one from 2007 are iconic.

But OLED doesn’t use a backlight. Each pixel lights up on its own, which is how OLED’s blacks are so utterly black, and how light bleed is so drastically reduced. So if there’s no backlight, does that mean the new glowing logo has a light source of its own? Yes, was the answer. Apple engineered a custom light source just to enable the logo to glow once again, without adding any additional thickness to the lid. Someone else in my briefing group asked why Apple would bother doing that. “Because it’s awesome,” was the answer, which I’m quoting exactly and fully. That was the entire answer. Because it’s awesome.

If you work in a dark environment where the glowing logo might prove a distraction, or if you’ve had your sense of fun surgically removed, you can disable the light. The light-up logo was a particular source of joy for Apple executives and product managers, including the fact that they managed to keep it entirely secret. One difference between this new glowing logo and the old ones from 1999–2016 is that when the light is turned off on this one, it just looks like the highly polished Apple logos from MacBooks since 2016. It doesn’t look, at all, like a light that is turned off. Thus, Apple was able to keep it from leaking by not enabling the illumination in the builds of MacOS that were used by employees who were testing preproduction models inside the company.

Pure awesomeness. Fun for the sake of fun on the back. The best laptop display in the industry — by a longshot — on the front. How utterly Mac-like.

In the late afternoon came the “Pro Workflow Showcase”, on the third and fourth floors of the building. (The second floor held a cafe and an outdoor terrace with a separate coffee bar. There was an entire other cafe downstairs on the first floor. The coffee, as usual, was pretty good, and the small plates tasty and fresh.) This showcase featured half a dozen demonstrations from creative professionals using the Mac in innovative ways to pursue their various crafts. Impressive demos from obviously talented artists, one and all.

U.K. filmmaking brothers Will and Ed Reid (a.k.a. “The Reids”) showed off their “4D Gaussian splatting” workflow, which allows them to capture immersive 3D scenes using a synchronized array of nine iPhones used as cameras. Portrait photographer Jeremy Cowart, from Nashville, demonstrated his crazily customized studio workflow, which allows him to capture and process hundreds of still photos per minute, with the background behind the subject shifting with each frame. Record producer Fab Dupont, who has worked with musicians ranging from Bad Bunny to David Crosby, mixed music live in Logic Pro. (Dupont was particularly fond of the touchscreen on the new MacBook Pros, which he repeatedly stated he expected to ignore.) From the fashion world, the wife and husband duo of designers Susan Fang and Orelio de Jonghe showed off an array of intricate 3D-printed clothing, gowns, and accessories. I found a new pair of eyeglass frames that, I’m told, suit my face. (Photo credit: Austin Mann.) And then, most delightfully and surprisingly, there was a two-section demo area from Japanese experimental botanist and “haute couture” florist Azuma Makoto. Azuma was the subject of Flower Punk, a documentary short by Alison Klayman for The New Yorker back in 2020 — which, now that I’ve seen his work up close in person, is high atop my to-watch list. Azuma uses the Mac in multiple ways. First, to design elaborate, beautiful botanical sculptures. Second, to design and engineer intricate contraptions and machines — research equipment — that allow him and his team to optimize and control the blooming of picked flowers. Third, to control that equipment in operation. The machines are as beautiful as the flowers. I commented on the mechanical switches. They beg to be flipped just to feel them click. After hearing my brief question translated into Japanese, Azuma’s partner Shiinoki Shunsuke answered at length, with great enthusiasm. They’re often asked, he said, why they design their custom equipment with analog controls, rather than control them entirely through software. They feel that the physical nature of the plants inside the machines demands physical controls to manipulate their environment. It’s like touching the flowers without touching them. A beautiful description of hauntingly beautiful works at the intersection of technology, biology, and art. It’s like Doc Brown from Back to the Future meets Martha Stewart.

Oh, and there was one other demo station. It was from a small filmmaking outfit named Industrial Light and Magic, and the primary demo was helmed by John Knoll. Knoll co-created an image editor for the Mac in 1987 with his brother Thomas, and has pushed the cutting edge of VFX across five decades at ILM. Both the image editor and the movies he’s worked on have achieved a fair degree of renown and success. When I saw him, I was nearly dumbfounded. It was all I could do not to walk up to him and say what my mind was screaming: “You’re John Fucking Knoll.” John Fucking Knoll, doing demos on the third floor. Holy shit.

Knoll brought with him an elaborate rig from ILM. A spaceship model from Star Wars: Skeleton Crew. A real physical model. Behind the ship was a very large curved LED screen — a smaller version of the cavernous “Volume” 75-foot chamber that ILM first used for The Mandalorian in 2019. A miniature Volume for miniature models. In front of the ship was an iPhone camera with a large lens mounted on a track. In front of the track stood Knoll, controlling the whole apparatus from a MacBook Pro (with logo aglow, natch). Knoll built this motion-tracking camera control system in his garage and wrote the firmware himself. Of course. He’s John Fucking Knoll. And he showed us how they use this system to shoot a practical spaceship model flying through hyperspace that is being rendered, live, on the curved LED behind the model. It’s all just captured in camera. The secret is genlock, which syncs the video rendered on the LED in front of the camera with the video being captured on the camera — synchronized precisely not merely to the millisecond but to the microsecond.

There are two questions I can remember being obsessed with as a child, that started me on the path to what ultimately became my career. The first was, “How did they make Star Wars?”2 Now here I was, seeing, just a little at least, exactly how they make Star Wars today — in arm’s reach of an actual goddamn ILM spaceship miniature. And a big part of the answer of how they make it today is, “With the Mac.”

By my count Apple held four major events this year. Two of them were the inviolable tentpoles of the annual Apple calendar: WWDC in June, and the iPhone event in September — both held, as usual, at Apple Park. WWDC is the all-encompassing software event for all of Apple’s platforms. The iPhone event is the iPhone event, with Apple Watch as the opening act.

Apple’s other two major events in 2026 were the no-event-title Neo introduction in New York in March, and last week’s “Pro and Tell” introduction for the new MacBook Pros in Los Angeles — both of them big, expensive productions, both held in big, expensive cities far from Cupertino.

Now consider Jason Snell’s Six Colors chart of Apple’s quarterly revenue by product line for the last five years, up through last week’s results for Q4 2026:

The green sliver represents the Mac’s share. Snell’s original chart is interactive — you can hover over it and get the specific breakdown for each quarter. The Mac’s share is consistently in the range of 7 to 9 percent for Q2, Q3, and Q4 each year. The iPhone is consistently around 50 percent in those quarters. In Q1 — the October/November/December holiday quarter — the iPhone jumps to around 60 percent, and the Mac drops to 5 or 6 percent. Year after year.

The Mac accounts for the high single digits of Apple’s revenue. High single digits, yes, but single digits. Yet two out of Apple’s four major events this year were focused entirely on the Mac. If you’re a pissant grump, you could argue that both of those events were wasteful, self-indulgent preening on Apple’s part. That the first one, for the MacBook Neo, was simply to announce a MacBook that cost $500 less than the previous entry point model, the MacBook Air. And the second one, last week in Los Angeles, was simply to announce MacBook Pros that cost $400 more than the previous ones, just to add touchscreen support that PC laptops have offered at lower prices for over a decade. All of this for a platform that doesn’t even account for 10 percent of the company’s revenue, with an operating system that ought to be put out to pasture.

What a miserably wrongheaded, ignorant, joyless take that would be.

These new MacBook Pros are worth showing off. What Mac users do and create on the platform is worth celebrating.

When I began closely following Apple, the Macintosh was Apple and Apple was the Macintosh. That hasn’t been true since the iPhone began its meteoric rise. Financially, Apple today is the iPhone, Services, and “everything else”.

But at the true center of Steve Jobs’s metaphorical intersection of Technology and the Liberal Arts, the Mac remains the heart and soul of everything Apple does, and responsible for so much of what users create with Apple’s products. We speak of people — both inside and outside the company — bleeding six colors. But the iPhone never had a six-color logo.

Apple has continuously adapted the Mac for changing times, changing technology, and a changing world, yet — for four decades — has kept it true to its original core. The Mac today is very recognizably the Mac to any user from any time in its illustrious history. Even touchscreen support, now, has been added the Macintosh way.

In 2010 I wrote “The Future of the Mac in an iOS World”. That piece has held up pretty well:

Here’s the short version of the “Mac is doomed” scenario: iOS is the future, Mac OS X is the past, and Apple, unlike most major tech companies, is strongly inclined to abandon the past in the name of the future.

You can’t really argue with that, can you? But the premise that the end is near for the Mac presupposes quite a bit about the near-term future of iOS. [...]

It’s the heaviness of the Mac that allows iOS to remain light.

When I say that iOS has no baggage, that’s not because there is no baggage. It’s because the Mac is there to carry it. Long term — say, ten years out — well, all good things must come to an end. But in the short term, Mac OS X has an essential role in an iOS world: serving as the platform for complex, resource-intensive tasks. The funny thing is, the best slogan to describe the Mac’s role is the same one it started with 25 years ago:

The computer for the rest of us.

I was only wrong then in fretting that the Mac might — perhaps — only have a decade or so yet ahead of it. Here we are now 16 years later and the Macintosh is more popular, more essential, more successful, and further ahead of its ostensible competition than ever in its 42-year history. Change comes slowly but it always comes.

The logo not only glows again. It might glow forever.

  1. I am reminded of the delightful story of how Microsoft wound up with the rights to “Start Me Up” for the Windows 95 launch. The Rolling Stones had theretofore never licensed a song for use in a commercial. Mick Jagger had always handled such inquiries not by saying “no”, but instead by quoting astronomically high prices. Microsoft asked about “Start Me Up”, Jagger gave them a no-way-they’ll-say-yes price (supposedly $12 million) and Microsoft simply said, “Great, that’s a deal.”  ↩︎

  2. The other was “How did they make Pac-Man?” ↩︎︎

item.content:encoded:
Why: Viticci digs into how Siri AI uses schemas, tools, and skills, a real look at Apple's agent architecture. (score 8)

From MacStories.

Earlier this week, I attended Apple’s online Apple Intelligence Group Lab, much of which focused on Siri AI. Much of the ground covered is available in Apple’s documentation, but the presentation included additional detail, which is worth highlighting, although I encourage you to watch the two Apple Intelligence Group Labs for more context and details.

The big-picture change that Federico explained earlier this week is that Apple is greatly expanding the actions available to Siri. Today, Siri AI’s natural-language abilities are limited to tightly defined domains like calendar, reminders, and messages. If a developer’s app doesn’t fit a schema (or hasn’t implemented an App Shortcut), Siri won’t be able to respond to a user.

Apple isn’t dispensing with schemas, but it’s loosening the reins, giving developers far wider latitude than before. Apple noted during the lab that schemas are still developers’ best bet for getting Siri to respond because Apple’s already done the work to ensure they work.

What’s changing is that Siri will be able to directly access developers’ App Intents that have been defined as tools. That’s a big change from today where a developer’s main access to Siri is through App Shortcuts, using a defined phrase that names the app. Instead, if a developer marks their App Intents as tools, Siri will be able to access those App Intents directly when a user makes a natural-language request, much like how MCP works with tools like Codex and Claude Code.

Other interesting tidbits about tools mentioned include that they’ll use Private Cloud Compute to process the request and that apps are limited to 40 tools.

Skills are a third brand-new way to access Siri that’s designed for more complex, multistep actions that can chain up to 32 tool calls. Like the skills you may be familiar with from Codex and Claude Code, Siri’s skills are Markdown instructions with YAML front matter that explain what Siri should do with certain requests. Xcode 27.3 beta also includes coding-agent skills that help developers add Siri support to their apps and test them.

Finally, beginning with iOS 27.3, which will ship in January if history is any indicator, developers will be able to customize the look of snippets of information from their apps similar to how Apple’s own apps’ content can look in Siri. As for tools and skills, those will be available to ship to the App Store in the spring.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Residential proxy software apparently running on the White House network, a striking security lapse with lessons. (score 8)

From The Verge.

Someone at the White House appears to be running software that could enable outsiders to rent access on the presidential network for just “a few dollars,” as reported by Krebs on Security and The Register. That’s according to findings from the security firms Layer3 Intel and Synthient, which discovered residential proxy activity on the White House network.

Just about anyone can rent access to White House IP addresses

Security researchers discovered residential proxy activity on the White House’s network.

Digital photo illustration of a laptop displaying a black and green image of the Capitol building, with ones and zeroes falling in the background.

Digital photo illustration of a laptop displaying a black and green image of the Capitol building, with ones and zeroes falling in the background.

A residential proxy opens up a way for people to rent access to a home IP address and route their internet traffic through it, allowing them to conceal where their activity is actually coming from. Some apps and browser extensions include third-party software development kits (SDKs) that put proxy nodes on a user’s device — whether users know it or not. Third-party services can then sell access to the residential proxies on users’ devices.

As noted by the cybersecurity firm Spur, people can legitimately use residential proxies for purposes like ad verification and quality assurance testing, but bad actors can also use them to bypass geolocation controls and defensive filters. Hackers have used residential proxies for all kinds of malicious activity, including to create botnets and carry out account takeovers.

At the White House, Layer3 Intel found that 28 residential proxy services routed traffic out of the network from October 5th to November 3rd. It notes that this activity typically happens between 5PM ET and midnight. “That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK,” Layer3 says. The SDK in question might be linked to the watch party app Rave, according to Synthient, which says the app “bundles 12 proxy SDKs into the platform.”

Synthient found “a number of Windows 10 and Windows 11 devices on the White House’s network beaconing to known proxy providers like Geonode, Infatica and Mellowtel.” As noted by Krebs on Security, Infatica is a proxy service founded by Vladimir Fomenko, the owner of King Servers, which was linked to 2016 cyberattacks on election systems in Illinois and Arizona.

Layer3 warns that the residential proxy is “public access,” adding that “anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it.”

item.content:encoded:
Why: Viticci on using the iPhone Duo as a pocket productivity computer. (score 7)

From MacStories.

As I hinted in my story about multi-window on the iPhone Duo, I find myself increasingly relying on Apple’s diminutive foldable as a pocket computer for getting work done with an external keyboard. It reminds me of the early days of iPad productivity: there’s something to be said about turning the multitasking limitations of the machine into a way to focus more and be less incentivized to switch between apps. Also, you know me: it’s fun to prove a point and show how you can get work done on an iPhone Duo if you want to.

As part of this, we’re dealing with the fact that we’ve received almost 600 submissions from developers about their iPhone Duo apps and app updates. I haven’t seen this kind of influx of new apps since the early days of the iPad (again, another parallel between these devices). John and I are working hard to make sense of all these app pitches, picking the ones that are worth our readers’ attention, time, and money. In the era of software abundance caused by AI, I think it’s more important than ever to test and curate software that wasn’t simply put together with two Claude Code prompts. This is why, rather than assembling an overflowing directory of iPhone Duo apps with no editorial curation, we’re going to write these old-fashioned roundups instead.

In the past two weeks since I’ve been testing the iPhone Duo, I’ve been impressed by the variety of productivity apps that have landed on the App Store. Most of these strike a fascinating balance of something in between an iPadOS and iOS experience – which, I guess, is the whole point of this new breed of pocket computer.

Below are some of my early favorites, which I’m using every day on my iPhone Duo. Expect more to follow over the next few weeks.

T3 Code

T3 Code is my favorite app for working with multiple coding agents in a single interface. I’ve mentioned this on AppStories before, but in case you haven’t listened: we’re working on two apps at MacStories, and both John and I are doing so almost exclusively in T3 Code. There’s so much that Theo and his team have gotten right here: from supporting multiple providers in the same UI and offering the best-performing ADE out there to an orchestration engine that can delegate to subagents and threads, T3 Code works beautifully in combination with Claude Opus 5.5. The app is fast, updated nearly every day, full of power-user details and fun touches, and even comes with its own built-in iOS simulator. It is, quite frankly, incredible that this team is beating OpenAI and Anthropic at their own game when it comes to building a desktop app for the modern era of software development.

T3 Code on iPhone Duo.

T3 Code’s own split-screen for subagents.

T3 Code’s own split-screen for subagents.

T3 Code, however, is also excellent on iPhone and iPad thanks to its (again, best-in-class) support for remote control. And as you can imagine, the app is particularly impressive on the iPhone Duo, which has become my favorite way to manage my agents and threads from anywhere I am. When the Duo is unfolded, T3 Code shows your threads in a left sidebar, where you can long-press one to get access to a variety of actions via a context menu. Your session takes up the majority of the display on the right, with toolbar controls natively relocated to the rightmost edge of the display, per Apple’s new conventions. If a thread has spawned any subagents, you can tap them to view their nested session, which will open inside the app in split-screen on the right. There is a dedicated button to dismiss the software keyboard (more apps should do this!), and the Duo’s semi-unfolded “book” pose is also supported.

Clearly, the T3 Code folks have spent a lot of time thinking about Duo interactions and remote control, and it shows. These days, I manage my agents running remotely on my Mac Studio exclusively via T3 Code. If you’re serious about this new kind of workflow and have an iPhone Duo, you can’t go wrong with T3 Code.

Sill

Created by indie developer Noah Saffer, Sill is a free and open-source Mac remote control utility that lets you stream your Mac’s display to an iPhone or iPad, with a couple of twists: unlike traditional VNC or RDP apps, it establishes a Direct Wireless connection between your Mac and iPhone; and, it lets you either stream the full desktop or specific Mac windows only, which get resized on the fly for whatever display you’re using.

For the technically inclined: Sill uses ScreenCaptureKit to capture your Mac’s screen contents, then uses an HEVC encoder to stream video at low latency, and instead of queuing video frames on a slow connection, it dynamically drops frames to ensure you can keep interacting with the Mac. There are lots of clever decisions behind the scenes in this app.

Once you’re connected and unfold the Duo’s display, you can see why I decided to highlight Sill in this roundup: it is unlike any other remote desktop utility I’ve tested in recent years, and it is one of the best examples of how to leverage the Duo’s inner display.

Sill is, arguably, the most impressive showcase of the iPhone Duo’s inner display so far.

Sill is, arguably, the most impressive showcase of the iPhone Duo’s inner display so far.

At the top of the screen, Sill features a horizontal bar that lets you scroll thumbnails of individual Mac app windows as well as a ‘Desktop’ button that instantly loads your full desktop instead. Pick a specific window thumbnail, however, and only that particular app gets streamed and resized to fit the Duo’s screen. At this point, you can touch the screen (or use Apple Pencil) to click, swipe to scroll, and long-press to invoke macOS’ contextual menus. The transition from full desktop to single app takes a second, and, in my experience with a good Wi-Fi 7 network and my iPhone connected to my wired Mac Studio over Tailscale on the same LAN, I’ve had good results with ‘Pro’ quality in the app (that’s a 40 Mbps stream, with Retina resolution and 120 fps).

There is a lot more to uncover here, though. You can long-press window thumbnails to reveal the classic “traffic light” controls, so you can minimize, full-screen, or close a window directly from Sill. There’s a built-in app launcher, which lets you quickly switch to apps open right now as well as launch anything from your Applications folder. You can natively invoke menu bar items, adjust the zoom level of every window with a swipe gesture, and tweak various settings to get the app’s performance just right.

Single-window mode.

There’s even an app launcher built in.

And if that wasn’t enough, Sill comes with one of the wildest and most useful implementations of screen sharing on a small display I’ve ever seen. I mean, just look at the app on the Duo’s outer display yourself:

Sill also makes the best use of the small outer display.

Sill also makes the best use of the small outer display.

I never thought I’d find logging into my Mac Studio remotely from the iPhone Duo’s outer display a pleasant affair, but Sill makes it possible. Noah Saffer’s app is an outstanding example of how to combine cutting-edge technology with device-specific optimizations to turn an old concept into something new and better than what we had before. I have no idea how this app is free, but if you like it, please consider making a donation to the developer on GitHub.

Marko

I’m always on the lookout for nice ways to quickly preview Markdown files – especially on iOS, where Marked doesn’t exist – and this new utility called Marko is worth a look.

The app works with Files’ native document browser, so anything that is accessible from the Files app – whether it’s an iA Writer document or a Markdown file stored in Working Copy – can be previewed from the app. Marko doesn’t have any custom themes for now, but the default appearance is minimal and elegant enough, and it gets the job done.

I like the extra options included in the app’s Markdown preview: you can summarize and ask questions about the current document with Apple Intelligence, read a document aloud with iOS’ built-in voices, and – critically for the iPhone Duo – view sections of a document in a left sidebar that opens next to the main Markdown preview.

Paste

My favorite clipboard manager for Apple platforms got a lot better on the iPhone Duo not because of new system frameworks that let it run in the background (sadly, that is still not the case), but because of Split View. On the Duo’s inner display, Paste now opens as a good-looking grid of your previously copied items and snippets visualized as rich thumbnails. The app is reminiscent of the iPad version in this mode, but what makes it special on the Duo is that you can tile another app next to it and start dragging and dropping content from Paste into a second app – a first for the iPhone.

The iPhone has supported inter-app drag and drop for a while now, but without native split-screen multitasking, you were always forced to keep holding onto a drag item with a finger, navigate back to the Home Screen or use the app switcher, find the target app, and only then drop the item. It worked, but it was awkward.

These issues are entirely remedied by Split View, which makes Paste fit into more workflows than ever on an iPhone. For instance, I can now keep Paste – which I also use to store reusable agent prompts – next to T3 Code on my Duo, tap an item to copy it, and instantly paste it in the ADE.

Paste continues to be the best-looking and most versatile clipboard manager for Apple devices, and I highly recommend setting it up on the iPhone Duo.

Calendaria

Created by indie developer Jorge Cohen, Calendaria is an interesting new take on the classic calendar app category in that it doesn’t aim to replace full-featured calendar clients, but instead focuses on being a good all-year planner that takes advantage of the iPhone Duo’s inner display.

You will not find the (many) features of Fantastical, Outlook, or, to an extent, even Apple’s Calendar app here. Instead, think of Calendaria as a companion utility to the calendar app you already use. There are three main views in the app: a year planner that shows you a summary of months and key events for each month in a left sidebar, with a vertical, scrollable stream of months and days on the right; tap an event on the right, and you’re taken to the second view, which is a more detailed monthly planner with a complete list of days on the left, and the currently selected day on the right; tap again, and the view advances horizontally again so you can pick between different events for the selected day and open an inspector panel for the selected event as the rightmost panel in the app. This kind of progressive, horizontal disclosure makes a lot more sense when you see it in action inside the app.

Calendaria’s first two pages.

Events and event details.

In fact, while you can alternate between views from the iPhone Duo’s right toolbar, my favorite way to use Calendaria is to swipe to fluidly move across views. Other touches I appreciate include the ability to write down a list of events in natural language and have on-device Apple Intelligence add them to your calendar, plus an option to “pencil in” events instead of fully adding them to your schedule.

I always appreciate it when someone brings new ideas to an established category of apps such as calendar clients; Calendaria is the first one I’ve tested in a while that actually gave me a reason to put it on my Home Screen.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Snell's two-week take on how iPhone Duo apps are shaping up. (score 7)

From Six Colors.

It’s hard to believe that I’ve been using the iPhone Duo as my iPhone and iPad for two weeks now, but here we are. I’m slowly working on a review when I’m not writing a zillion other things related to Apple’s very busy product season.

One thing that’s really changed over the last two weeks is the support for the iPhone Duo among my most-used apps. When I first set it up, the good apps were few and far between. But today, I’m actually surprised when I hit an app that hasn’t been updated to support the Duo. Apple’s data bears this out, as this statement (supplied to Six Colors by Apple) from Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Developer Relations Susan Prescott points out:

It’s been wonderful to see how quickly developers have embraced iPhone Duo, and we’re grateful for their creativity and innovation. Today there are well over 100,000 apps built for iPhone Duo already live on the App Store, and thousands of optimized apps are being added to the store each day. In the last month alone, thousands of developers have joined us for workshops in 19 cities around the world to experience iPhone Duo firsthand and bring updated apps to their users. The enthusiasm has been incredible, and we’re excited to see the pace of updates continue to accelerate as more and more apps optimize for iPhone Duo.

Here are a few of my favorites thus far: Marco Arment’s Apple Pencil-savvy sketch app Fineliner, Aniline’s social-media client Indigo, Balazs Varkonyi’s RSS client ReadKit, Yoav Zoldan’s TV tracking app Skipper, Cross Forward’s revived weather app Check the Weather, and the YouTube TV app for some election-night multitasking.

Why: Chinese intelligence reportedly recruited an AI exec to spy on Nvidia's CEO, a notable security story. (score 7)

From The Verge.

China’s intelligence agency recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted her to glean information about American AI chips and “potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia’s, and Alice Huang also has “relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A.I. chip industry,” including leaders at Gigabyte, the NYT says.

China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang

Nvidia’s CEO is reportedly the target of a ‘Chinese spy plot’ for intelligence on American AI chips.

Last week, the NYT reported that Jensen Huang was seen as the target of a “Chinese spy plot” and shared details about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang’s relationship, but the information that China’s MSS had recruited her is new.

The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang, was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his “interactions” with Alice Huang.

item.content:encoded:
Why: On your always-include list. (score 10)

From Cliff Mass Weather Blog.

This weekend, we will "enjoy" the meteorological trifecta of winds, coastal waves, and substantial precipitation.


First, the winds.

The forecast sea level pressure for Sunday at 10 AM predicts a strong 994 hPa low center to west of the Washington coast.


The associated winds (below) are impressive, with sustained winds of 50-60 knots to the south and west of the low center.    This is known as the "poisonous tail" in the weather business.


Such strong winds over a large area (large fetch) will produce large waves that will reach our coast later this weekend (see below).   These waves will climb to 45 feet offshore and over 20 feet on our coast.

There will be good wave watching on the Washington coast on Sunday.

As the low moves northward up the coast on Saturday and Sunday morning, wind gusts will increase along the Washington coast and   over the western Washington interior  

The forecast gusts at 4 AM Sunday are shown below.  Strong gusts (50 kt and more) on the coast; 30- 45-knot gusts in the interior, particularly near the water.



The UW runs perhaps the most sophisticated wind prediction system in the country for Seattle City Light (called WindWatch), and it is predicting 40 mph gusts in Seattle on Saturday night and early Sunday. (see below)


As the first major blow of the season, with lots of vegetative growth over the summer, there will be power outages.
 
My "pro-tip":  charge up your electronics and lights on Saturday.  You won't regret it.

Finally, there is the wet part of the upcoming weather.

Below is the predicted precipitation accumulation through Monday at 4 AM.  Very wet in the Olympics and the northern Cascades.  Plenty elsewhere.  Reservoirs will begin to fill.


This is just the beginning of the wet/stormy season in the Northwest, with a lot more on the way.   Typical November conditions, and there is no going back.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Post-quantum hybrid TLS lands in an Azure edge service, right in your lane. (score 9)

From Post Quantum Crypto Tech Blog articles.

Introduction

Azure Front Door provides a global edge for modern applications, combining content delivery, HTTP load balancing, TLS termination, acceleration, web application firewall capabilities, Azure DDoS protection, and access to Microsoft’s global network. Because many applications already terminate public TLS at the Front Door edge, it is a high-leverage point for post-quantum cryptography. You can learn more here.

The Azure Front Door team has enabled hybrid post-quantum key establishment for inbound TLS 1.3. Front Door can now negotiate TLS groups that combine classical elliptic-curve exchange with NIST-standardized ML-KEM.

When a client supports hybrid post-quantum TLS, the session uses quantum-resilient key establishment; otherwise, configurable classical fallback preserves compatibility if needed.

The immediate risk is harvest now, decrypt later (HNDL): adversaries can retain traffic captured today until a cryptographically relevant quantum computer can break its key establishment. Moving edge ingress to hybrid TLS 1.3 reduces this long-term confidentiality risk without requiring every Azure hosted application and Azure services behind AFD to change at once.

What the AFD team built

Azure Front Door terminates client-facing TLS at the edge and uses a separate connection to Azure services. PQC currently protects the client-to-Front Door TLS 1.3 segment; extending it to Azure service connections is the next engineering phase.

For the client-facing segment shown in red below, Front Door supports Post Quantum groups such as SecP256r1MLKEM768 and X25519MLKEM768 while retaining classical ECDHE groups for compatibility.

The default order prefers a mutually supported hybrid group, then falls back to approved classical groups.

How Azure Front Door works in this model

Clients connect to a nearby Azure Front Door point of presence, where Front Door terminates TLS, applies routing and WAF policy, accelerates and caches eligible content, and routes traffic across Microsoft’s network to Azure services.

This managed edge capability lets customers begin PQC migration without immediately updating every backend.

Over time, Azure Front Door will extend hybrid PQC TLS 1.3 From Azure Front Door Edge locations to Azure services/client applications connections as they roll out their support.

Cryptographic design

TLS 1.3 hybrid key establishment combines classical elliptic-curve exchange with ML-KEM. The session remains protected if either component remains secure, enabling migration without prematurely abandoning classical cryptography.

Managed Standard and Enhanced policies balance NIST-aligned elliptic curves (P-256 and P-384), internet compatibility, and customer control. A Custom policy permits explicit TLS group choices when needed.

Validation and performance

Validation used three gates: compatibility testing, synthetic load testing, and matched production A/B testing. Together they confirmed safe fallback, measured processor and handshake impact, and isolated the incremental ML-KEM cost.

Synthetic tests showed low CPU overhead (less than 1%) for the primary ML-KEM-768 groups, while matched production testing found no measurable CPU regression for X25519MLKEM768 against an X25519 control.

Customer configuration and rollout

TLS 1.3 hybrid PQC is enabled by default; no customer action is required. Customers can additionally configure AFD TLS policies - including protocol versions, groups, and cipher suites - to balance security and compatibility.

User Interface

Below is an example of the new UI in the Azure Portal, notice how you can select a custom policy so you can choose to support only PQC groups, only classic, or PQC and classic, depending on your security versus compatibility requirements.

 

Podcast Episode

In Azure Security Podcast episode 134, Michael interviews Vlad and Kunal from the AFD team about the PQC TLS 1.3 update. The episode is available in all the usual podcast sources, or you can go here: https://azuresecuritypodcast.azurewebsites.net/episodes/Episode0134.html 

Summary

Azure Front Door now supports. by default, TLS 1.3 hybrid ML-KEM key establishment, with classical fallback, managed customer policies, and staged compatibility and performance validation.

This mitigates the most critical harvest now, decrypt later (HNDL) risk of encrypted data going over the internet between the client to the AFD front-end, protecting your back-end Azure resources.

Thanks

Big thanks to all the people how reviewed this post and provided corrections, clarifications and input.

  • Vlad Polyakov – Azure Front Door
  • Jessie Jia – Azure Front Door
  • Kunal Samant – Azure Front Door
  • Varun Chawla – Azure Front Door
  • Amit Srivastava – Azure Front Door
  • Maks Gotkowicz – Cloud Solution Architect

item.content:encoded:
Why: OpenSSH flaw exploited within hours of disclosure shows how fast the window closes. (score 7)

From The Hacker News.

Threat actors are attempting to exploit a recently disclosed security flaw impacting OpenSSH that can enable sign-ins to accounts that have no password set, according to Previdian.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score: 8.1) and codenamed SSHole (or *sshole), impacts Linux systems that run OpenSSH on the musl C library with Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) disabled, including Alpine Linux's default OpenSSH server configuration.

An unauthenticated attacker can supply an oversized password to access accounts that are deliberately configured without usable passwords, without having to steal credentials or SSH keys. The issue, discovered by security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, has been addressed in OpenSSH 10.6p2.

The underlying issue dates back to a patch introduced in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210. Under specific conditions, the password-handling behavior in OpenSSH mistakenly interprets a failed password-hashing operation as successful authentication by producing the same value ("*") used to indicate that an account with password disabled at the system level.

An attacker can trigger the vulnerability to authenticate to certain password-disabled accounts using an arbitrary password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long, causing the hash attempt to fail and returning an asterisk. The sshd daemon then compares with the asterisk stored in the account's password field, leading to a successful login.

To be clear, successful exploitation requires at least one account with an asterisk (*) as its password hash. It does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes.

"A successful SSHole attack grants access with the compromised account's existing permissions," Safe Security said. "For enterprise, the consequences of SSHole depend on the privileges of the compromised account."

"While unauthorized SSH access is the immediate impact, attackers may also gain access to deployment credentials, application secrets, and connected infrastructure, potentially enabling lateral movement or service disruption."

Image Source: Safe Security

It's worth noting that the vulnerability does not affect Dropbear, glibc-based Linux distributions, non-Linux systems, and systems that check passwords through PAM.

Threat intelligence firm Previdian said it observed the first exploitation attempt less than nine hours after the CVE publication, adding it has confirmed successful root access on a honeypot running Alpine Linux and OpenSSH. Telemetry data shows a total of eight exploitation attempts from an IP address geolocated to Japan.

"The observed source IP, 89.116.89[.]18, used oversized passwords to bypass authentication and ran reconnaissance commands including id, uname and hostname through non-interactive SSH sessions," Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

Affected users are advised to install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or their distribution's patched package, and then restart sshd. Alpine is also recommending that users investigate "Accepted password for" log entries involving accounts that should not accept password logins.

"Look in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password (alpine, root, or any key-only user)," Alpine said. "Review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys on exposed machines. If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised."

Google News,
