Apple today announced a new high-end MacBook Pro, which is available in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes. The new device has a PROLED XDR display that supports touch gestures, and a glowing rear Apple logo. Pricing on the MacBook Pro starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399 for the 16-inch model. Apple says the MacBook Pro has the "world's best display in a pro laptop." The PROLED...

Thursday October 8, 2026 1:31 pm PDT by Juli Clover

Apple will introduce new OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro models and an OLED iPad mini "on or around" Tuesday, October 27, reports Bloomberg. The launch will also include an M6 14-inch MacBook Pro and an M6 iMac. The October 27 follows Apple's October 13 debut of a new smart home hub, a revamped Apple TV 4K, and a refreshed HomePod mini. Earlier this month, MacRumors reported that Apple would do ...

Neo. And would have been more next year if it weren't for the price hikes.

I'm not buying a Mac until my current one completely dies. I even have an older one that I think I can save with a new battery and will probably do that.

People buying to get ahead of the price increases to come next year. The MacBook Neo helped a lot. But with its new higher price, will sales continue at the same rate? I'm not so sure.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Logic Pro's AI feature is subscription-only, a notable shift in Apple's pro app pricing. (score 7)

From MacRumors: Mac News and Rumors - All Stories.

According to Apple's full release notes for version 13.0 of Logic Pro for Mac, released today, the new AI-powered Intelligent Assistant feature requires an Apple Creator Studio subscription for $12.99 per month or $129 per year. In other words, the feature is not available in the $199.99 one-time purchase version of Logic Pro.


Apple's fine print on the Logic Pro release notes page:
The intelligent assistant (beta) requires an Apple Creator Studio subscription, a Mac with Apple silicon, and macOS 27 or later.
Indeed, the release notes for the one-time purchase version of Logic Pro for Mac version 13.0 do not mention Intelligent Assistant.

The subscription requirement was not mentioned in Apple's announcement last month:
The assistant (beta) in Logic Pro for Mac requires macOS 27 Golden Gate or later on an Apple Intelligence-capable Mac and is available in U.S. English only.
Apple customers who are growing tired of features being locked behind a subscription will obviously be disappointed to learn this news.

Logic Pro's Intelligent Assistant likely requires a Creator Studio subscription because it uses cloud AI models. In a support document, Apple said the feature will have monthly usage limits, with expanded usage available for a fee.

Apple says the Intelligent Assistant is powered by a combination of Apple-built and third-party AI models. The feature is designed to help creators "navigate production workflows, start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project." Except for creators who opted to pay $199.99 upfront for Logic Pro, that is.
Tags: Apple Creator Studio, Logic Pro

item.content:encoded:
Why: Claude can now read your bank accounts, an AI trust and security question worth knowing. (score 7)

From The Verge.

Anthropic has a new pitch for managing your personal finances: let Claude do it instead, with a new Personal Finance feature that connects it to your bank and card accounts via the Plaid bank bridging platform. You can ask the chatbot “where did my money go this month,” for example, and it’ll create an overview with a breakdown of spending by category, including rent and utilities, shopping, and food. Claude can also answer broader questions around what bills are left before your next payday, if you can afford big purchases like holiday trips, and how much money you could be saving each month.

Claude AI can plug directly into your bank account

With access to your bank account via Plaid, Anthropic’s chatbot will try to explain where your money is going and what you can afford.﻿

Its access is read-only, and with Plaid facilitating the connection, Claude doesn’t see your banking passwords and your bank doesn’t have to deal with unvetted AI bots crawling around your accounts.

Claude can’t move, manage, or invest your money, according to Anthropic, and it “isn’t designed to give investment advice.”, but it can see the bank’s name, account names, account type, the last four digits of the number associated with it, your balances and credit limits, and up to two years’ worth of your transaction history.

If you choose to give it access to all that, Claude can explain financial terms you don’t understand and answer questions about your balances and transactions.

Personal Finance in Claude is rolling out in beta this week to Claude Pro, Max, and Ultra plan subscribers in the US. Anthropic’s announcement follows OpenAI introducing a similar feature for ChatGPT in May, which also plugs into your bank accounts through Plaid. Allowing AI to have oversight into your finances might ring some alarm bells, but according to the sign-off in Anthropic’s press release, it’s just the beginning:

“Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust. We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it.”

item.title: 360: Turn On The Lights. Desa’a. AI vs Hurricane. Coffee.
item.author: Fix The News
item.description:
Why: Fix the News roundup of hopeful, data-driven progress. (score 7)

From Fix The News.

Best drunk black from a ceramic cup, on a springtime Wednesday morning.
item.content:encoded:
Why: Fix the News roundup of hopeful, data-driven progress. (score 7)

From Fix The News.

You’re reading the world’s best and most comprehensive source for good news. Check out our library of stories. Listen to the podcast. Meet our charity partners.

Let’s try something new…

Humanity knows how to prevent most maternal deaths. We know what good maternal healthcare looks like. But in some parts of the world, the people delivering that care are working without something we take for granted: reliable electricity.

Nowhere is this a bigger problem than in Nigeria, where a woman giving birth faces a risk of death more than five times the global average. Women arrive at clinics carrying their own candles or lanterns. Midwives use the torches on their mobile phones to deliver babies. And when complications arise in the middle of the night, healthcare workers find themselves trying to save lives in the dark.

But there’s a solution. An organisation called We Care Solar has developed something called a Solar Suitcase: a compact, solar-powered system that gives maternity clinics reliable light and essential equipment, even when the grid fails or doesn’t exist.

For US$4,500, one clinic can be equipped with a system that provides power for more than a decade, including installation and battery replacement.

We supported We Care Solar’s work in Sierra Leone a few years ago. Now we’re hoping to bring their reliable power to four more healthcare centres in Nigeria.

Our goal is to raise US$18,000, and we’d love your help.

In the lead-up to Giving Tuesday on the 1st of December 2026, we’re inviting Fix The News readers (and friends!) to come together to help Turn On The Lights. We’ve set up two ways to contribute:

🇦🇺 In Australia? Donate via Myriad Australia. It’s 100% tax-deductible for all Australian residents.

Donations from Australia

🇺🇸 In the United States or anywhere else? Donate via Every.org. It’s 100% tax-deductible if you’re based in the US.

Donations from US and rest of world

We’ll be running this campaign here in the newsletter for the next few weeks. Every donation helps bring light to places that bring life, and every cent goes directly to purchasing and sending the suitcases to these clinics.

This week’s top stories


Lenacapavir, the twice-yearly HIV-prevention injection, is moving closer to cheaper access in low-income countries. Indian generic manufacturers Hetero and Dr Reddy’s have committed to making it for $40 per person per year in 120 countries covered by Gilead’s licensing agreements, compared with the US annual list price of $28,218. Chemists in Virginia have also developed a simpler synthesis route that reduces raw-material costs by roughly 30%. Dr Reddy’s version received FDA tentative approval this week, with first supplies expected before the end of the year and broader availability in 2027. But this extraordinary medicine will still need funding if it is to reach the estimated 20 million people worldwide who need it. Health Policy Watch / Unitaid / VCU News / PubMed

Barbados has eliminated mother-to-child transmission of HIV. No baby born there between 2022 and 2024 caught the virus from their mother. Of pregnant women, 98% now get antenatal care, 98% are tested, and 98% of those with HIV are treated. PAHO

Reality keeps beating the IEA’s predictions on solar. Energy researcher Auke Hoekstra has plotted every International Energy Agency outlook since 2002 against how many solar panels the world actually ended up making. It’s one of the most famous graphs in clean energy research: the forecasts keep levelling off, while production keeps climbing. Needless to say, the IEA’s 2025 outlook is going to be wrong too. RenewEconomy

Vaccinating mothers for RSV is keeping babies out of hospital. Pooled data from the US, UK, Argentina and France show babies whose mothers got the jab in pregnancy are 74% less likely to be hospitalised with related lower respiratory tract infections. The mother’s antibodies cross the placenta, so the baby is protected from birth. England saw 63% fewer bronchiolitis admissions in babies under three months than expected (and that’s with only 55% of mothers vaccinated). Gavi

Don’t say we don’t bring you the important news! A multi-country citizen-science study on what makes coffee enjoyable (yes, really) found that people say coffee tastes best black, during spring, in the morning, on Wednesdays, and when drunk from ceramic cups. You’re welcome. Nature

All five of life’s genetic letters have turned up on a second asteroid. Japanese scientists analysing dust that the Hayabusa2 probe brought back from asteroid Ryugu have found adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine and uracil, the five bases that spell out DNA and RNA, in roughly similar amounts. In 2023 the same team had found only uracil. NASA’s samples from Bennu, a different asteroid, held all five too (we wrote about that in Edition 349). That means the ingredients are probably common in space; how often they turn into life is still anyone’s guess. Nature Astronomy / ScienceDaily

Ecosystems covering 2.5 million km², about the size of Alaska and Texas combined, are now under restoration. A report launched at COP17 counts projects in 149 countries, with more than a million jobs created from the 35 World Restoration Flagships, big government-backed projects the United Nations holds up as showcases. “Restoration” covers a lot of ground, from replanting native forest to simply stopping whatever was wrecking a place and letting it heal, and about half the global total is in China.

In Brazil, Paraguay and Argentina, more than 300 organisations are stitching the shattered Atlantic Forest back together into corridors for jaguars and golden-headed lion tamarins. In South Africa, the World Bank has launched a $120 million bond to pay for restoring spekboom thicket, a scrubby succulent landscape that feeds elephants and black rhinos. And in Canada, Indigenous communities and Parks Canada have begun restoring hundreds of kilometres of salmon streams; salmon numbers are up at six of the seven sites. UN News

The most eye-popping of these World Restoration Flagships is in the middle of a war zone. Ethiopia is restoring the Desa’a forest, one of the country’s oldest remaining dry Afromontane forests, which straddles the northern regions of Tigray and Afar about 45 km from Mekelle, Tigray’s capital. From 2020 to 2022, Tigray was the centre of a civil war between Ethiopia’s federal government and Tigrayan forces: the restoration work carried on through it, with small groups, constantly changing location, getting around by bicycle and donkey when the fuel ran out. “We were asking communities to plant trees and carry out activities, but at the same time, we were afraid to do so because of airstrikes or drone attacks,” says Aklilu Negussie Mekuria, WeForest’s country director for Ethiopia. A peace deal was signed in November 2022, but fighting broke out again this September.

So far the project has brought more than 230 km² of degraded land under restoration, holding an estimated 500,000 tonnes of soil in place and capturing 1.9 million cubic metres of rainwater a year (about 760 Olympic swimming pools). It has created nearly 16,000 jobs, around 60% for women, and backs local livelihoods like beekeeping (Tigray honey, project manager Yemane Gebru notes, is very expensive). Endangered Nubian dragon trees are being revived, leopards are returning, and the area shelters ‘church forests’ and some of the oldest Christian sites in the world. Mongabay / WeForest

Brazil has published the first global roadmap for moving off fossil fuels. Its COP30 presidency wrote it after oil producers blocked the idea at last year’s Belém talks. It asks for national transition plans by 2028, renewables investment under way by 2030, and a 2031–33 push to speed up the switch. “We don’t need more negotiations,” said André Corrêa do Lago, the COP30 president. Nobody is bound by it, but with the Iran war keeping oil north of $100 a barrel and solar panels costing a fraction of what they did a decade ago, the plan looks a lot more viable than it would have a few years ago.

A separate group is going further: at Santa Marta, Colombia, in April, nearly 60 countries formed a “coalition of the willing” to write their own national phase-out plans, and Germany, France and the Netherlands have already published theirs. Reuters / The Guardian

Fossil gas is losing its grip on six of the world’s biggest markets. Fossil gas’s share of power fell this year in China, Japan, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, South Korea and Turkey. In the Netherlands it was just under 32%, down from nearly 60% in 2020. Reuters

Also… no energy transition huh? Someone might want to tell the coal, oil and gas companies in Colorado.

Bangladesh has wired electricity to 99% of the country, and is now going after the last remaining hills. A $175 million Asian Development Bank loan approved in September will pay for at least 88,000 new household connections in the Chattogram Hill Tracts, aiming to lift access there to 68% by 2032.

Google’s AI just beat the physics on a hurricane. In early October, conventional models predicted that Hurricane Isaias would head west towards Louisiana. Google DeepMind’s model correctly put it on the western Florida Panhandle, where it came ashore near Destin as a Category 2. “By far and away, the best performing computer model that we’ve ever seen,” says meteorologist Michael Lowry. NPR

Visits to China’s archaeological parks have risen nearly fivefold in four years. The country’s 65 national archaeological site parks, from 7,000-year-old Neolithic villages to imperial tombs, drew 97.74 million visits in 2025, up from 20.97 million in 2021. Some of that is just a rebound: 2021 was a pandemic year, and between 2016 and 2020 the parks averaged about 40 million visits a year, back when there were only 36 of them. But interest really has grown. In 2021, state broadcaster CCTV livestreamed the excavation of the sacrificial pits at Sanxingdui, and the site’s very strange bronzes went viral (one standing figure looks remarkably like the Japanese superhero Ultraman, which the internet did not fail to notice). Splashy new site museums followed, at Sanxingdui in 2023 and at the Yin Ruins, the last capital of the Shang dynasty, in 2024. Xinhua

Read more

item.title: MacBook Pro with PROLED review: You could even say it glows
item.author: Six Colors
item.description:
Why: Snell review of the first touchscreen MacBook Pro, the big Apple launch of the week. (score 8)

From Six Colors.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is, like its name, a bit overloaded with meaning. Its banner feature is its impressive tandem OLED display, a first on the Mac—but most people will instead remember that display because it’s also a touchscreen.…
item.content:encoded:
Why: Snell review of the first touchscreen MacBook Pro, the big Apple launch of the week. (score 8)

From Six Colors.

The back of a MacBook with a glowing white Apple logo sits open on an outdoor wooden table at dusk, with white chairs nearby and dark silhouetted trees against a deep blue sky behind it.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is, like its name, a bit overloaded with meaning. Its banner feature is its impressive tandem OLED display, a first on the Mac—but most people will instead remember that display because it’s also a touchscreen. Advances in Apple silicon are usually a major part of the story of a new MacBook Pro, but not this time around—these new laptops are powered by the same M5 Pro and Max chips introduced on the MacBook Pro earlier this year.

So, yes, the real story here is the screen—but what a big story that screen is! In fact, it’s two big stories.

OLED and everything after

Let’s start with that OLED display, because it’s clear that this new laptop redesign (the first since the M1 era in 2021) was inspired entirely by the desire to move the MacBook Pro off of mini-LED backlit LCD panels and onto OLED at last.

Let’s be clear: The “old” MacBook Pro display is spectacularly good. But there’s only so much even Apple could do with that technology. OLED is just superior, in so many ways: it’s thinner and lighter, uses less power, and every single pixel emits light on its own, so you can have spectacularly bright areas with pitch-black pixels right next door. (The contrast ratio on the PROLED XDR display is ten million to one.)

The display really is impressive. Obviously, its primary target audience will be creative professionals who can take advantage of the wide color gamut (P3+Adobe RGB) and high dynamic range to create work without any fear that they’re not seeing exactly what they expect to see. For me, a person who mostly works in typed words and audio, well, it sure was something to pull up 4K HDR movies on the PROLED XDR display.

I was also impressed by just how bright the screen can get. Obviously, bright HDR content will be incredibly bright, up to a peak of 2000 nits. But I was also impressed with its brightness in standard dynamic range. In bright environments (think: direct sunlight), the display is actually capable of cranking up SDR brightness to 2000 nits, because even in direct sunlight, you do need to see your computer’s display to get anything done.

Since this is an OLED display, there could potentially be lifespan-limiting issues like burn-in. Apple says the laptop is continuously monitoring each pixel on the display and applying compensation to reduce long-term burn-in and retain as much consistency and precision as possible.

Just as those M1 MacBook Pro models introduced us to the “notch,” a camera and sensor cut-out smack in the middle of the menu bar, the PROLED MacBook Pros introduce the Dynamic Island to the Mac for the first time. In other words, the “notch” is now a small circular cut-out from the display. Rather than leaving it as blank space, Apple has taken a page from iOS and turned it into the Mac’s own Dynamic Island. (It’s still dead center in the menu bar, though, so menu items will need to leap over the island as they did the notch.)

Spotlight and Siri AI are now animated as emerging from the black blob that is the Dynamic Island. Now Playing appears up there, too, and you can click1 or tap2 on the Dynamic Island to expand it and get playback controls. Shared Live Activities from your paired iPhone should also appear up there, rather than in the menu bar itself, as they do on other Macs.

I’m a big fan of subtle, ambient information presentations that inform you about things happening on your devices. That’s why the Dynamic Island was such a fun approach to turning a problem (an unsightly camera cut-out) into a useful feature. The notch never really did anything—it was just a dead zone. The Dynamic Island serves a purpose and the MacBook Pro is better for it.

The other killer feature

I’ve written so many words about OLED, and yet we still haven’t gotten to the other huge feature of this new laptop design: The new 14-inch model is a full half-pound (about 15 percent) lighter, and the new 16-inch model is 0.7 pounds lighter. The new 14-inch model weighs three pounds, putting it closer to the MacBook Air in weight than the old 14-inch MacBook Pro.

I know, I know, all of this dramatic display technology and the fact that you can touch it and it does stuff, and I’m talking about weight?

Well, yes. Because unless you leave your laptop on a stand all day long, weight is one of its most important features. I spent maybe fifteen years commuting on public transportation with a laptop in my backpack, and it’s what made me fall in love with the MacBook Air. Because every ounce saved mattered. Even when carrying the laptop around the house or office, it’s just more pleasurable to move that thing if it’s light. To shave a full half-pound off in one go is just remarkable. I don’t hate toting my M4 Max MacBook Pro around when I need to, but I notice those 3.5 pounds, especially given my history with the MacBook Air.

But to get a high-performance laptop at three pounds? (Okay, if you get the M5 Max chip it’s 3.1 pounds, but still…) To cut 15 percent off the weight of a fairly mature laptop without sacrificing any battery life? It’s a design choice that deserves to be celebrated.

You can touch it

Then there’s the feature that probably seems like a bigger deal than it actually is: touch. If you care about the Mac, this is an incredible moment, the first time Apple has made a touchscreen Mac after decades of resistance. (Yes, people were agitating about touchscreen Macs back in the 2000s.) Fifteen years ago, Steve Jobs kicked off what has turned into a long parade of Apple executives who have had to explain why Apple just didn’t see any value in adding touch to the Mac, in the face of a load of PC laptops that offered it.

It’s complicated. The early PC touchscreen laptops weren’t really very good. Mostly the touchscreen was something a commodity PC maker would add so it could check a box on a feature list, even if it wasn’t particularly useful or well-integrated into Windows. At least some of Steve Jobs’s disdain for touchscreen PCs came from being asked why Apple wasn’t jumping off the same bridge as the PC makers. He drew from the same well of poisonous feelings he used to explain why Macs didn’t have Intel Inside stickers on them.

Which is not to say that there haven’t been interesting PCs that really took advantage of the touchscreen. The thing is, they weren’t conventional laptops. They were tablet PCs, or maybe convertible laptops with screens that flipped around or folded flat, so that you could interact with them via touch (or stylus) with better ergonomics than reaching out over a keyboard to touch a vertical display.

Apple, meanwhile, set about building some of the most popular touchscreen devices in the world, starting with the iPhone. Apple has made its own “tablet PC” since 2010—but it’s an iPad, not a Mac.

The fact that Apple’s selling its first touchscreen Mac in late 2026 is a bit hilarious. I suspect that at some point, corporate dogma took over and it became impossible internally to champion adding touch to Mac laptops. Pretty much every Apple executive has appeared in public and declared it a bad idea at some point. Also, after one of the world’s leading tech companies goes a couple decades without adding touch to its laptops, doesn’t the pressure build up a bit?

Oh, after all this time, you’re doing a touchscreen? This better be good!

Meanwhile, over the last couple of decades—and this is a trend Apple is directly responsible for—everyone who uses technology has become used to interacting with touchscreens on a regular basis. And once you spend enough time touching pieces of glass, it becomes second nature—to the point where I have absolutely reached up to tap or scroll on my laptop screen only to have to remind myself that it’s a Mac and it doesn’t work that way.

I’ve also used my iPad Pro with an attached keyboard and trackpad enough to recognize that, even when I’m driving that device like it’s a laptop, sometimes I will find it easier to just reach out and touch. It’s natural, it works, and it’s nothing to be afraid of.

So finally Apple is ripping the bandage off and embracing touch. In doing so, it really had two choices: Invent an entirely new paradigm for the Mac interface, one based on touch… or don’t do that and just make sure the existing Mac interface works fine if you use your fingers instead of a trackpad.

It chose the second one, and rightly so. If this new MacBook Pro was some weird convertible device with a fold-back screen and Apple Pencil support, adding a load of new touch features and gestures would make sense. But Apple has wisely chosen not to inflict a series of edgy and opinionated design decisions on its loyal base of professional users. I hope Apple does make a weird convertible MacBook Studio someday! But it wouldn’t be a MacBook Pro.

So, yes, you can touch the MacBook Pro’s screen and stuff happens. For the most part, I found I was using it the same way I used my iPad’s touchscreen when it was configured like a laptop—for reaching out and idly scrolling, tapping, maybe pinching and zooming. The touch affordances are subtle—tapping the menu bar will space out menu items a bit, tapping on the “traffic light” window controls will cause them to zoom out, iPad style, to make them clearer targets. Selecting text is accomplished by a double-tap (the rare gesture that is different from the usual iPhone/iPad playbook), and tapping and holding on an item in the Finder makes it lift upward, indicating you can drag it. (It also brings up the context menu, which is a little awkward but does the job.)

Would I expect someone to perform detailed brushstrokes in, say, Photoshop using their finger? No, I would not. But I do think that app developers may well appreciate being able to test their apps right on their laptops, complete with support for all the iPhone and iPad multitouch gestures. And there are undoubtedly other apps that can benefit from proper multitouch support—Apple demonstrated a Logic plug-in that allowed you to operate multiple control surfaces at one time with different fingers, something that’s impossible if you’re using a normal Mac with a single pointing device. That was pretty cool.

But touch seems like a niche interface so long as you’re touching a screen that’s upright, hinged behind a keyboard. I like that Apple has done this, and I hope it brings touch support to all its laptops over the next few years. But it’s a nice-to-have additional input mechanism, and that’s all. It will not dramatically change the way you interact with a Mac, nor should it. But given that we live in a world where just about every device supports touch, Apple needed to get over itself and make the Mac work with touch. It did, and that’s great.

(Oh, and if you hate the idea of touch, you can just turn it off in Accessibility settings and pretend this laptop is exactly like every Mac laptop that has ever come before it, no different in any way except maybe that the screen’s really nice.)

Always be branding

Back in the late ’90s, someone (maybe even Jony Ive?) had the bright idea to put a translucent Apple logo on the lid of the PowerBook G3, so that the Apple logo would glow. A couple of years later, Steve Jobs ordered that the logo appear right-side-up when the laptop was opened, and an era of rooms full of glowing representations of the Apple brand began.

Unfortunately, we can’t have nice things, and in the mid-2010s, among many other bad decisions, Apple changed its laptop logo to be a beautiful polished metallic shape—but one that didn’t light up.

Well, the MacBook Pro with PROLED has a polished metallic logo on the lid… and yet, somehow, when you turn on the laptop, it glows in the old-school style. You might think that this is a trivial detail barely worth mentioning, but that’s the point exactly. This is an independently controlled light source (there’s no backlight on an OLED screen!) that can, according to Apple, be turned off via a setting if you don’t want it to be seen.

Apple went to the trouble of engineering a glowing logo on the lid of the MacBook Pro—a whimsical bit of nostalgia that also coincidentally is pretty good branding—despite the fact that it has no real practical purpose. I love that. Apple has gotten really good at being ruthlessly efficient and at creating wildly popular tech products and accompanying services that have allowed it to generate nearly half a trillion dollars in revenue in the past year. But there needs to be more to that story. Apple should also maintain a level of whimsy, a touch of humanity, a desire not just to have a successful business but to truly surprise and delight its customers.

Bringing back the glowing Apple logo is a tangible example of Apple staying in touch with its soul. I love it. More like this, please.

That’s all there is… for now

It’s really strange to have a new generation of MacBook Pros with a new design—and yet no new chips. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, this is because Apple canceled the M6 Pro and Max chips in order to get to an even more impressive M7 generation due next year. I like the aggressiveness of that move, but it does have the side effect of making this particular product introduction a bit awkward.

Anyway, here are some test results. They’re pretty much the same ones you saw back in March:

Yes, the M5 Pro and Max chips are powerful. If you really needed them you could’ve gotten them in March, but they’re still good. (The next ones will probably be way better, though.) They’re just not new.

It’s so easy to focus on new chips when new Apple products come out that it’s almost refreshing to be forced to focus on everything else. Fortunately, the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display has a lot more going for it than a normal upgrade does.

We only get a major revision to a major Mac product line every few years, and this is a big one. The new OLED display is spectacular, especially if you need the best color or the most dynamic range—or a display capable of cranking way up in bright conditions. The reduced weight is an enormous improvement that shouldn’t be overlooked. That you can tote an M5 Max chip around in a three-pound laptop (okay, fine, 3.1 pounds for that model) is incredible. The Mac Pro in your backpack is just a whole lot lighter.

And, yes, there’s a touchscreen too. It’s a development that seems momentous, and yet is almost an afterthought compared to what else is going on with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR. Touch has been added tastefully and I hope it spreads to the rest of the MacBook line sooner rather than later. (And yes, if Apple would like to do a weird convertible laptop at some point, bring it on—as its own separate thing.)

This is the second MacBook Pro product release in one calendar year. It’s a little weird, like both revisions took a half-step forward rather than taking the single stride forward we’re used to from Apple. If you’re in the market for a new MacBook Pro, for an extra $400 you can get a dramatically better display, and lighter laptop, with touch—if any of those matter to you. The good news is, this design will probably be with us for the next several years, so if now is not the time for you to take the plunge, relax—there’s always next year.

  1. Apple has added a delightful animation for when the pointer moves under the Dynamic Island that looks like it’s being sucked into a black hole. ↩
  2. I’m going to need time to process this change. ↩

item.content:encoded:
Why: OpenAI AI pipeline found and patched 948 Linux root escalation bugs, relevant to security and AI. (score 8)

From The Hacker News. Also covered by The Verge.

OpenAI on Wednesday detailed a pipeline that employed an upcoming cyber-focused artificial intelligence (AI) model to validate and patch 948 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Linux for $1.2 million in API costs.

"Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access," the AI company said.

The findings build upon 24 LPE exploits that OpenAI revealed were discovered by its GPT‑5.5‑Cyber model back in June 2026. The latest research turns this process into an agentic pipeline comprising five stages -

  • Vulnerability discovery, where agents identify high-value audit targets (i.e., parts of the codebase that are security-relevant and reachable by low-privileged users) and look for candidate findings
  • Dynamic validation, where agents attempt to reproduce each candidate in a sandboxed environment and preserve runtime evidence
  • Exploitability assessment, where agents test whether validated vulnerabilities could be abused to facilitate information disclosure or LPE and devise a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit
  • Patch generation, where agents generate patches for the identified vulnerability
  • Human review, where security researchers review the exploit, patch, and proposed severity before it's reported to the maintainers

"In a run in mid-October 2026, our pipeline using an upcoming cyber model dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities [within 30 hours] and generated PoCs for 291 information leak vulnerabilities and 948 working local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits for a commonly used Linux distribution," OpenAI said.

"The total run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or $1,279 per LPE exploit. To the best of our knowledge, the agents in this pipeline discovered and used at least 10 novel Linux exploitation techniques."

At a high level, these include -

  • Two new persistent elastic objects to spray objects inside the target kernel cache
  • Two new page grooming techniques to improve exploit reliability
  • Five new data-only techniques to obtain privilege escalation directly or via an arbitrary write
  • One technique that involves arbitrary type confusion

The development is once again an indication of how frontier AI is redrawing the contours of cybersecurity, accelerating vulnerability discovery and exploitation, and at the same time helping defenders reliably address defects, albeit through additional instructions and iterations, before attackers can use them, and make it "cost prohibitive" for bad actors to exploit software.

In a report published last month, VulnCheck categorized AI-assisted vulnerability discovery as a "growing risk category" that turbocharges novice hackers, who now require little to no technical expertise to detect software vulnerabilities.

The access to AI models is not just limited to defenders, but also bad actors who can leverage the same capabilities to discover and weaponize new zero-days and expand the pool of viable targets with minimal effort.

According to insights from Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), the number of vulnerabilities disclosed per month has more than doubled, rising from 5,045 in January 2026 to 10,740 in August 2026. The number of vulnerabilities classified as high-risk has surged from 131 disclosures in January 2026 to 350 in August 2026, a 167% growth.

"The widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has almost certainly led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities," the U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said in an assessment published Tuesday.

"Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an N-day vulnerability, and have made patching a quicker process. However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses."

The NCSC also pointed out that organizations will have to evolve their internal patching and testing processes to meet this new pace of vulnerability discovery.

"Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal," it added. "Cyber capabilities are now used for a broader range of activity due to the lower risk involved, making it easier for adversaries to access information and use it operationally."

OpenAI said the rate of vulnerability discovery by frontier models needs to be matched by automated patch generation to secure software and to limit the exploitation window.

"With human expert-guided iteration, we believe AI-generated patches can be functionally correct, aligned with existing coding styles, and robust to attack variants," OpenAI said. "For the near and medium term, having access to a low-privileged account on an operating system that isn't up-to-date on its latest available patches should be considered functionally equivalent to root access for a well-resourced threat actor."

Google News,

item.content:encoded:
Why: Apple will scan public iCloud links for harmful content, a security and privacy policy shift. (score 8)

From The Hacker News.

Apple has revealed that it plans to start checking public iCloud links for harmful content starting with iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3.

The change specifically applies to scenarios where users share iCloud content, such as photos in iCloud Photos or files in iCloud Drive, by sharing a link and making it accessible to "Anyone with the link."

When users choose this option, it makes the content accessible to anyone who has the link, including Apple, the iPhone maker said.

"Starting in version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content," it said in a support document published Tuesday.

Apple also explicitly noted that sharing an item that can be accessed by Anyone with the Link disables end-to-end encryption (E2EE), even if the owner or the recipients have turned on Advanced Data Protection, an optional setting that secures iCloud Backup, Photos, and Notes using E2EE.

That said, it's unclear what prompted this change, what Apple considers as "harmful content," and whether these checks will also be applied retroactively to previously generated links, as well as any new links created before the 27.3 updates are officially rolled out later this December.

The tech giant has also warned that if users attempt to upload harmful content, it can be removed or deleted at any time.

"Apple may also take action against your Apple Account, including blocking or disabling your Apple Account, blocking the ability to create a new Apple Account with the associated email address or phone number, or if necessary, involving law enforcement," it said.

Google News,

item.content:encoded:
Why: Six Colors on the 27.3 Siri AI features and developer preview. (score 7)

From Six Colors.

Apple’s 27.3 Developer betas added some major Siri AI features to Safari, but that’s not all. There’s also the Siri AI Developer Preview, which Federico Viticci analyzed in detail, finding it to be a sign that Apple really is executing fast on its AI development game plan:

You don’t roll out this kind of expansion two months after the launch of iOS 27 unless you truly have a flexible orchestration layer and modern harness that can make the assistant more useful simply by virtue of giving it more tools.

It’s been a slow burn for Siri AI over the past two months, especially since it was always a bit unclear what would work and what would break when using it inside apps. I’m curious to test the updated architecture over the next “few months” (per Apple), and I’m now very confident about the fact that Apple is building a Siri Agent for iOS 28.

Apple lost two years by fumbling the Apple Intelligence roll-out. It’s good to see that it still has a serious sense of urgency and isn’t hibernating until WWDC 2027.

Go to the linked site.

Read on Six Colors.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Hackett linking Pierce on how the touchscreen MacBook Pro feels in use. (score 7)

From 512 Pixels.

David Pierce at The Verge:

I keep forgetting the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display has a touchscreen. I’ve been testing this new laptop, one of the most impressive Apple has ever created, for the better part of a week. I can’t stop noticing some of its other features: the slimmer design, the improved display, the Dynamic Island that somehow catches my eye more than the notch ever did. But I keep forgetting that as I go about my day, I can now reach out and poke the screen.

Come to think of it, that might be exactly what Apple intended. Steve Jobs said touch laptops were a bad idea; some subset of users demanded one anyway. Now the MacBook Pro has one. But not in a way that meaningfully changes the laptop experience. There have been a few times I have found the touchscreen genuinely useful, better or more intuitive than anything I could do with a trackpad or a mouse. But to call this “the touchscreen MacBook Pro” just doesn’t feel right. It’s the latest evolution of Apple’s most powerful laptop — and oh, it happens to have a touchscreen.

item.content:encoded:
Why: Krebs on residential proxies on White House staff devices, a real security lesson. (score 7)

From Krebs on Security.

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

To imagine that culture and society and events out there have no impact on the lives we […]
item.content:encoded:
Why: Godin on Washington and isolationism, short and thoughtful. (score 7)

From Seth's Blog.

In his farewell address, he said, “Our detached and distant situation invites and enables us to pursue a different course.”

It’s easy to fall in love with the idea that we live in a detached and distant situation. To imagine that culture and society and events out there have no impact on the lives we live.

The coal plant across the country, the goings on in the CEO’s office, the impact of tech on our culture… none of them are very far away. We have more leverage and connection than we want to admit.

Insulation is scarce. Technology, the competition and the shifts in media come for us, whether we seek them out or not.

It doesn’t pay to fret about things we can’t influence, but we might be able to influence more than we realize.

Perhaps isolation was useful for George. It’s clearly not true now.

item.title: The Reviewers Are Crazy; the iPhone Duo Is Fantastic
item.author: Spyglass
item.description:
Why: Kafka's contrarian take on the iPhone Duo pushes back on the reviews from a favorite writer. (score 8)

From Spyglass.

Some thoughts on the iPhone Duo...
item.content:encoded:
Why: Kafka's contrarian take on the iPhone Duo pushes back on the reviews from a favorite writer. (score 8)

From Spyglass.

The Reviewers Are Crazy; the iPhone Duo Is Fantastic

There I was on iPhone Duo launch day in an unfamiliar place: no new device in hand. Sure, I went to an Apple Store to try it out — which was sort of a wild experience in and of itself, with nearly all the Duo demo units out of battery from so much usage — but thanks to Apple’s inventory (mis)management here, even pre-ordering within seconds of availability wasn’t fast enough to secure one on day one. So I had to wait.

And while I normally don’t read any reviews ahead of forming my own thoughts on new products, with the Duo I was more curious than normal for obvious reasons. Still, I kept things high-level with some quick scans of headlines and key takeaways. And my sense was that reviewers were actually pretty mixed on the device. Some were downright negative. An unholy thought crept into my head: should I cancel my pre-order? Is this just a colossal waste of money?

Well, I didn’t. And I’m glad I didn’t. Because I think those reviewers are crazy.

The iPhone Duo is an incredible device. I ended up getting mine a few days after the launch and I wanted to use it for a week before writing anything just to make sure I wasn't the one who was crazy. I honestly think I've liked using it more each day.

I’m not quite ready to say it’s the best iPhone Apple has ever made, but I’m close. Certainly closer to that than the reviewers seem to be towards putting it on the other end of that spectrum! Three simple things hold me back. First, I don’t like knowing that I don’t have the best possible camera system. Second, it’s heavy and feels fairly bulky when folded. Third, a lot of software, namely third-party software, is still playing catch-up here.

That last point was what many reviewers focused on for obvious reasons. But it’s also a little silly to knock the device for that because not only will this change with time, it’s already changing, fast. Google Maps was updated today, for example. Still no Gmail, but I would imagine that's any day now. Anthropic and OpenAI were ready to roll on day one if you’re into those kinds of things, which I am. Even Meta, the company which famously took 15 years to launch Instagram for iPad, was there from the get-go. Meta!

To the second point, there's no denying the bulk and weight. It's just physics and it's what takes the most getting used to. I actually quite like the feeling in hand when folded — it’s easier to hold in some ways with more depth — but carrying it around, it’s sort of like dropping a brick into your pocket. The most beautiful brick ever. But actually it’s more like half a brick. The older variations of foldables look far more like bricks with their elongated shapes. Yes, this is more akin to a passport. One belonging to the most-traveled person in the world.

The camera system will not change with time – well, at least until a second Duo launches with an upgraded system, of course. But I'm just not sure how much that matters to "regular" iPhone users because the Duo camera system is obviously more than good enough for everyday usage. That said, the camera system may have been a factor in the iPhone Air not being a hit out of the gate, so you can't discount it to zero – especially when you're paying $2,000+ for this device. But to me, it's more about that knowledge in the back of my head rather than any issues with the camera day-to-day.

Form

Let's go back to the form factor. I love it. I love it both folded and unfolded, but I especially love the optionality. I've been using it mainly as you would expect: in terms of sheer number of interactions, most of the time it's folded. But for overall usage in terms of time spent, I imagine unfolded wins. That feels fairly natural. If you're going to do something fast, you do it on the outer screen. If you have some time or a longer task, you'll probably open it up.

What I didn't expect is that I would actually like using the outer screen quite a bit. Yes, there are some mild confinement issues with apps not updated yet – and oddly, Safari, which obviously was updated, but is apparently being fixed to let it spread out more on the wider screen – but after years on iPhone Pro Max models, I had forgotten how much I appreciated smaller screens. Not always and not for everything, of course, but that's why having the larger screen on the inside is key. For many tasks, having a massive display – including those found on the 'Max' iPhone models – is overkill. And I find the smaller screen focusing, in ways.

Sure, I wish the Duo were thinner when folded. But again, I actually quite like holding it, heft and all. And I'm definitely faster at typing on it than I am on a "regular" iPhone. I sort of suspected this would be the case in a move to a more BlackBerry-like aspect ratio, but it's sort of wild just how much faster I am typing on that outer screen. I don't know if it's just the perfect shape for my particular thumbs, but it's hands down one of my favorite surprise upgrades here.

Less great is the aforementioned pocketability. But it's a trade-off: a massive slab for that squat brick. That too will change with time, of course. Eventually we'll clearly have Westworld-style thin, folding devices. For now, this is just an intriguing taste of what's to come.

Function

Unfolded, the iPhone Duo is not as much like the iPad mini as I would have expected going in. The biggest difference right off the bat is obvious, but subtle: most of the time when you start using an iPad mini, you're probably doing so in portrait mode. With the Duo, once unfolded, you're probably using it in landscape mode. From there, counterintuitively, whereas the iPad at first looks sort of like "a big iPhone", the Duo is something different. Thanks to the clever unfolding UI, the device opens up to reveal not only your iPhone homescreen as you were just looking at it, but also your widgets, which are normally a right-swipe away on the left-hand side. This naturally makes those widgets more first-class citizens here. And while you could of course put widgets on your homescreen, on this new left screen, you can only have widgets there. Again, it's a subtle, but key usage difference.

Swiping left gives you a more standard grid of apps, since it showcases your first and second pages of apps. But even that looks different due to the new right-side dock. I'm still getting used to that change, but I think it suits the UI well given the shifting screen dynamic. I wish you could add a fifth – or even sixth? – app to that dock, but maybe that's just the iPadOS and macOS user in me talking. In general, I find the way Apple has shifted the controls to the right to be clever and intuitive.

That said, while I'm right-handed, I tend to use my iPhone with my left hand for whatever reason. This does make reachability an issue for the dock when folded – which Apple is also addressing, and already has a "reachability" fix in beta – but unfolded, you're probably using two hands, or tapping with your index finger, so it's not an issue.

Screening

The inner matte screen is such a brilliant maneuver by Apple. Not only does it help hide the crease (which you can more easily feel than see except at certain angles in certain lighting), it just looks and feels great. I even like that it's different from that outer screen just to give you more variety in terms of how you use the Duo. I've been a full convert to their "nano texture" screens on other Apple devices and I'm happy it's here on this iPhone. It's clearly something that every other foldable manufacturer is about to copy.

Apple Pencil support was just turned on with the latest iOS update and it's certainly a nice to have – in particular on that big, matte screen (though yes, it works on the front screen as well). The Pencil itself feels comically large compared to the Duo, it's almost as if they should have made a 'Pencil mini'...

Back to fingers, the single biggest complaint about the Duo from reviewers may be the lack of Face ID. It's one thing that it's not on the Mac yet – no, not even the so-screen-focused-that-they-put-it-in-the-name new 'MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR' – it's another to take it away from the iPhone. I don't know, maybe I am crazy here, but I honestly don't miss it that much? One of the first things I did upon setting up the Duo was register four fingers (and one side-of-finger, per internet instructions) and... I just haven't had an issue unlocking it fast? Maybe not quite as seamless as Face ID, but that fails for me at times too. I realize this reads a bit like cope, but I honestly just don't think it's that big of a deal. Maybe it's because I'm a die-hard iPad mini user who is used to it?

Far more annoying to me are the volume rockers being at the top of the device. That's just awkward (as it is on the iPad mini too). AirPods volume-swipe FTW. I miss the 'Action' button a bit, but not all that much to be honest. I'm glad the 'Camera' button remains.

The Case

I opted to get the 'Folio' case because I refuse to deal with adhesives (I still sort of can't believe that Apple is okay with this option, but there must have been no other solution, at least for the front screen). I've actually never had a folio-style case for the iPhone and I thought I might dislike having the screen covered, but I actually quite like it. It looks smart, like a small notebook you'd carry around. And the 'TechWoven' material feels good in hand – certainly better than 'FineWoven'! A clever extension mechanism allows it to stay in place when unfolded. And when using it folded, you can place the front cover around the back. Yes, this adds to the bulk, but once you're at this point, why not "own" it? It is, of course, less than ideal when taking pictures, but also just not that big of a deal. And the whole case is extremely easy to take off thanks to magnets rather than adhesive.

Make the Case

I honestly love this device. I strongly suspected I would like it – unlike, say, the HomeView, which I just don't really understand – because I've been using other foldable devices for a few years now and I like those too. And the iPhone Duo is like those, but with Apple polish. Using it alongside the Pixel Fold (I've had a few generations now, most recently last year's 10), the difference in overall quality feels very night and day. I hate to use Apple's own talking points, but one really feels like two phones tacked together versus the Duo which just feels like something new and purpose-built.

Because, of course, it's not just the hardware, it's the tweaks to the software that Apple made to make the experience different in those subtle ways. And it feels like it's perhaps right place/right time for a smaller on-the-go screen to be viable thanks to the plethora of other devices – Apple Watch, AirPods, soon perhaps smart glasses, etc – that we increasingly are also wearing and using. As crazy as it sounds right now, in a few years, it might seem weird to see giant slabs of glass sitting in front of everyone on tabletops. I'm not saying there won't be smartphones – there will be – I'm just saying they may start to look different. Perhaps foldable. Maybe smaller. Maybe even like that device in Her! And while the Duo may not be the first step along the way, it's the first one that's likely to push the industry in that direction in a massive way.

The Masses

All of that points to the future. But what about the present? Are the reviewers largely right that the iPhone Duo isn't ready for most people right now? Perhaps simply because of the price – though Apple took preemptive steps to try to mitigate such concerns, clearly. But from a sheer product perspective, this is an excellent device, right now. It's certainly better than a lot of Apple's other first attempts at new product categories.

In a way, it is like an 'iPhone Ultra' – one of the long-rumored potential names – perhaps all-but in camera. And it has the price to match that distinction. Will that change with time too? We'll see (don't hold your breath).

For now, it's just a great device at a high price. The Apple Way.

One more thing: I won't lie and say that I don't have any anxiety about folding and unfolding the Duo. Even a week into doing it constantly, I live in persistent fear that "Crackgate" will strike. This is hopefully unfounded, but we just don't know the scope and scale of the issues yet other than Apple acknowledging some "small number" of problems. (And no, I'm not using it in the 'tent' or any other bent position yet.)

item.content:encoded:
Why: Viticci explains how Siri AI's 27.3 expansion changes what apps and agents can do on iOS. (score 8)

From MacStories.

Siri AI in iOS 27.3 beta.

As part of the release of the 27.3 developer betas yesterday, Apple announced a substantial expansion of the capabilities of Siri AI. As you recall from my iOS 27 review two months ago, Siri AI launched with support for a limited subset of app domains based on schemas that Apple specifically optimized for the first version of Siri AI. In a major reversal for a mid-cycle update to Siri AI, that limitation is entirely going away: the updated Siri AI will instead work with any kind of app that supports any custom App Intent – as long as the developers do the work of modernizing their App Intents and integrating with Siri. Effectively, though, any app can work with Siri AI now, and Apple calls this the Siri AI Developer Preview.

From Apple:

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order. For complex requests, we’re also introducing skills to let you teach Siri AI how to combine several actions into a single experience. And Siri AI can now surface any entity in the Spotlight semantic index, not just the ones that fit an existing schema.

We started rolling out these new capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

The short version is that Siri AI is no longer a specialized, domain-specific assistant but can instead work with any type of app. The longer version is that this also means Apple had to fundamentally improve the Siri AI harness during the iOS 27 cycle to support these new capabilities. For example, the updated Siri AI harness (called “agentic planner” in iOS 27’s code) can now dynamically read skills supplied by apps at runtime when performing a complex action. That’s right: Apple is also fully supporting the Markdown Agent Skills spec now with the ability for developers to supply a variety of skills in their apps to give Siri more precise instructions for longer actions and complex requests. Apple explains:

Siri is aware of your app intents and entities but may need additional guidance on which intent to use for a complex request, so your skill needs to provide that information. For example, tell Siri which intent to use for which step in a person’s complex request, the order to perform the app intents, how to disambiguate intents and entities, or what not to do.

Here’s an example from Apple of a complex request:

Siri can find custom content from one app, transfer it to a specified app, and perform an action. For example, somebody might request “Hey Siri, send my favorite sneakers to my partner in name of a messaging app.” Siri finds sneakers that the person added to their favorites, understands who the partner is, finds them in Contacts, then sends the sneaker information to them using the messaging app.

And here are the new tools included in Siri AI’s agentic planner, as parsed from the iOS 27.3 beta firmware:

  • view_skill: This one loads an app’s instructions for a specific skill.
  • get_skill_response: Lets the system receive a skill’s result or follow-up question.
  • available_skills: Metadata listing the skills Siri can choose from, with their names and descriptions (but not the full body text).
  • activated_skill_instructions: Metadata containing the loaded skill’s instructions for the current turn.

Apple itself is already shipping three skills in the first beta of iOS 27.3, including one that teaches Siri how to select and edit text in the Notes app.

Apple’s skill for editing text in the Notes app.

Apple’s skill for editing text in the Notes app.

Interestingly, as I was reading the skills Apple made for file management, I noticed that Apple was referencing bash commands in them. Amusingly, it uses these commands to teach the model about App Intents-based tools and their equivalents as shell commands:

Of course, the model appreciates being explained new tools in the context of bash commands.

Of course, the model appreciates being explained new tools in the context of bash commands.

Like in most frontier AI agents and assistants these days, skill descriptions are read by Siri when needed (something Claude pioneered with dynamic skill loading), and if Siri determines that a skill can be useful, then the longer body text of the skill will be read, too. This obviously adds a bit of latency to the Siri request since the assistant needs to process up to 10,000 more characters (the upper limit of a skill length per Apple’s spec). You can see this in action when asking Siri to insert some text after a specific word in a note in iOS 27.3: the action will be completed successfully, but it’ll be slower than the typical Siri AI query since it involves reading a skill upfront.

Here are a few more details on skills, as explained by Apple’s developer documentation:

You can’t use app skills to enforce deterministic behavior. Instead, app skills provide additional information that Siri AI uses to respond to complex requests. Siri AI doesn’t sequentially perform the tool intents that your skill lists.

And:

Siri reads the Markdown body only after it determines that the skill matches a request.

When a person makes a request, Siri AI determines how to respond to the request. Siri considers the app skills you provide by reading the metadata you include at the top of the SKILL.md file.

There’s even a new feature to test and simulate how Siri will respond to user queries via App Intents and skills, called Siri Evaluations:

Start with a few scenarios that use simple, direct requests to confirm that your integration works end to end, alongside trying requests with Siri on a device. Then build a broad set of scenarios that reflects the many ways people phrase requests, and include indirect, incomplete, and unexpected wording. Because Siri’s responses can vary between runs, run the set more than once, and improve your intents, their parameter names and descriptions, and your App Skills until more of the set passes, and passes consistently.

The rapid expansion of Siri AI is both surprising and obvious.

It’s surprising because I did not think Apple had it in them to iterate on the assistant so quickly without – as far as we know – a more powerful model than what they showed back in June and launched in September. This goes to show a) how serious Apple and John Ternus (more below) are about Siri AI and b) how much new value can still be extracted from existing models with better scaffolding around them.

It’s also obvious because, as I argued in September, it was clear that Apple had to adopt some of the AI industry’s established standards and patterns if they wanted to stay relevant in this race. Or, as I wrote:

In the AI scene, companies move fast and break things. Apple needs to move fast without breaking anything – not anymore, at least.

Generalizing App Intents and adopting skills are obvious moves that will exponentially diversify Siri’s output and capabilities inside apps. I’d argue that extended support for user-defined memories should be coming next (rudimentary support for Siri memory about past conversations was added in 27.2); likewise, users should eventually be able to save their own skills as repeatable instructions for Siri. Skills and memories are the backbone of modern agentic loops in products such as Muse and Dots; if Apple wants to lay the foundation for a Siri Agent next year, they have to start from where the rest of the AI industry first began nearly a year ago.

Speaking of which, here’s John Ternus, who was asked about Siri AI and agents during this week’s earnings call:

Look, first and foremost, we’re incredibly excited to launch Siri AI alongside the latest generation of Apple Intelligence features. Siri has long been popular with our users with more than two and a half billion requests every day, and with Siri AI, we really have the kind of the Siri that we always wanted. It’s primarily request-based today, but as we talked about at WWDC, it’s built on a modern orchestrator-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand its capabilities over time. As far as agentic capabilities, we think these are promising tools for users. We just want to make sure that users are aware of what they’re giving access to. We want to make sure this is done in a way that protects security and privacy. So we’re pushing really hard on that with Siri AI, but we’re also really encouraged by the fact that Apple devices, we think, are the best places to use all forms of AI.

You don’t roll out this kind of expansion two months after the launch of iOS 27 unless you truly have a flexible orchestration layer and modern harness that can make the assistant more useful simply by virtue of giving it more tools.

It’s been a slow burn for Siri AI over the past two months, especially since it was always a bit unclear what would work and what would break when using it inside apps. I’m curious to test the updated architecture over the next “few months” (per Apple), and I’m now very confident about the fact that Apple is building a Siri Agent for iOS 28.

item.content:encoded:
Why: How the record $6.3 billion Binance heist was months in the making, a breach with real lessons. (score 8)

From Michael Tsai.

Rafael Nam:

The massive $6.3 billion cyber heist suffered by crypto exchange Binance last week may have taken place in only about twenty minutes — but the attacks were months in the making.

That’s according an initial assessment released by Binance on Tuesday about how it suffered the world’s biggest-ever cyber heist by hackers the FBI has identified as being a North Korean state-sponsored unit.

Molly White:

At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets. Tether announced they had frozen at least $1.567 billion of the stolen USDT, and Circle has frozen around $800 million of stolen USDC. World Liberty Financial froze the $27 million in USD1 stolen by the attacker, and the Arbitrum ethereum layer-2 network froze an additional $30.5 million that had moved to its network. The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion.

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who is legally not allowed to have any active role with the company [I98] yet still has remarkable amounts of inside knowledge into its inner workings, posted on Twitter less than an hour after the theft that “User funds are safe!”, adding early estimates of how much Tether and Circle had frozen.

[…]

Binance keeps an emergency insurance fund in case of exploits or other crypto disasters. Its most recent balance report puts it at around $1.3 billion. Unless more is recovered, Binance will either fail to make users whole or dip into its own balance sheet — potentially to the tune of 10 figures.

Jessica Lyons (Hacker News):

In September, another software engineer was contacted via a “legitimate job-hunting platform” by someone purporting to be a project director who arranged a series of job interviews for the Binance engineer with the fake company. During the first round - a live video interview with the engineer and a fake HR rep - the interviewer “shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust,” according to the report. “This was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches.”

The second interview with someone purporting to be the CEO of the phony company was conducted on a “popular social chat app,” and toward the end, the CEO instructed the engineer to download an “assignment” containing a malware-laced code repository. The code executed on his work computer during the setup process, which kicked off a series of unauthorized activities.

According to Binance, the malware replaced a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version, which executed commands and established communication with an attacker-controlled external server. The attackers also took steps to hide the malicious script and evade detection, and it worked. Binance’s endpoint security tools did not immediately detect the malware.

gandreani:

A lot of people are focusing on how irresponsible the engineer was about using the work computer. That’s obviously an issue but the bigger failure mode to me is the Engineer C’s container deployment token.

That’s a huge red-flag. In a company of this size, the deployments should be via CI only. CI isn’t just to increase the speed and reliability of deployments but also to provide a clean room to build the software! Even if it’s a token that was copied and pasted temporarily, the systems in place should not have to require this type of 1. copy 2. paste 3. remember-to-delete the token from my PC.
